DOROTHY DONEGAN
NEA Jazz Master (1992)
Interviewee: Dorothy Donegan (April 6, 1922 – May 19, 1998)
Interviewer: Jeannie Cheatham with recording engineer and interviewer Matt Watson Date: April 5-6, 1998, Beverly Hills, CA Description: Transcript, 107 pp.

I’m here with Dorothy Donegan, my name is Jeannie Cheatham. This woman has been my idol for all these years and I finally get a chance to really talk to her about her life. Dorothy, the first thing I’d like to ask is where were you born and when?
I was born in Cook County Hospital, Chicago, Illinois, April 6, 1922.
Where’d you go to school?
I went to Willard School, DuSable, Chicago Musical College, Chicago Conservatory…oh, a lot of schools.
It sounds like it. I would like for you to tell us, who was your first influence when you were a little girl.

Well, coming up, I had studied with Alfred Sims, he was my teacher. And then, I would get into fights with children. So, one day they chased me up three flights to Portia and Fredrika Goodlow’s house. And they were pianists, I didn’t know this. So I said, “Let me in because the kids want to beat me up.” So they let me in. So they heard me play. They said, “Mama, she can play.” They decided I should go downtown to Lillian Brown.
So that was the way you started playing?
Well, yes, of course I could play before I got to them, though.
Tell me your first instant at the piano when you recognized that that might be your instrument.
I used to gig with the musicians, Roscoe Cotton (?)
I mean when you were a little girl…
When I was eight years old, I could play all of Ellington, and I think I recognized it then.
I understand.
And I used to stay with some of the drunk musicians who played very well like Raymond Walters and people like that. Sonny Thompson. And that I didn’t know I would gorilla off of them (laughs).
Could you tell me, the first lesson you took, what did your mother pay your teacher?
One dollar, that’s all they got.
Very expensive.
That was a lot of money in those days. But they took it. Alfred Sims was a good teacher, he had a lot of patience with me. But I would learn all he knew in about a year or two.
Yes. In some context, can you explain to people what one dollar meant? How much did one pound of sugar cost?

I guess a pound of sugar cost a nickel. A dollar was worth three dollars now. ‘Cause now if I get lessons I have to pay you $75 or $50. Of course, I don’t get lessons, I get coached. “Do this,” and “Do that.” “Dorothy, a little bit more point.”
Tell me one thing more. Did anybody in your family object to your practicing?
No, except the neighbors downstairs, ‘cause sometimes I’d be stomping and they could feel it underneath, you know. But nobody stopped me.
Did you have to put a sock on your foot?
No, I could stomp. Don Shelly (?) said, “That woman sure can stomp.”
Well, tell me, did you play in any orchestras when you went to school?
I played in Roscoe Cotton’s band. But that didn’t last long. Because I think playing with a band was something Mary Lou Williams could do better than me.
Why?
Well, I like to solo and that’s not good with a band. It’s better to accompany rather than solo. So, I’d be soloing and taking off by myself.
You were what you would call a diva.
Oh yes. Yeah, I like to steal a show mostly.
Well, did your mother take you around to places to play when it came time for you to go into the nightclubs?

Yeah, I was chaperoned by my mother and my brother. We’d play for fish frys and rent scuffles. The ladies sometimes couldn’t pay their rent so they’d give a party and sell fish sandwiches for 15 cents. Chicken (sandwiches) for the same. And that’s how they made their rent payments.
How about this—did you have special dresses even then to perform in?
No, my mother would get me a pretty good dress, you know. Then, you could get a whole outfit for $15.
Even the shoes?
Yeah, the shoes were $2 or $3. We’d go to Rothschild’s. I didn’t know a thing about Neiman Marcus, ‘needless markups.”
Tell me one thing more, when did you get your first pair of long hose to wear on stage? What year was it?
Oh my goodness, I guess in the 40’s when I played Orchestra Hall. I played that all by myself and sold it out.
That’s when you got your first pair of long stockings?
I guess I was wearing them before then. I’d steal a pair of my mother’s, you know.
Did you have to get a color for yourself, or was it hard to find the correct color during those times?
No, I could find a color. They were all beige you know.
Yes. Did you have to dye them with tea?
No, not then.
Not then?
I also liked to wear black stockings but that came at a later time.
Yes. When you first started playing in nightclubs, did they have the separate dressing room for the lady performers?
I think so. We had separate dressing rooms for the lady performers.
Did you have to dress in there with the dancers?
Yeah, I dressed with the dancers. They used to say, “Now we have jazz in the house.” I said, “Now you have talent in the house.” (both laugh)
Yes. Can you tell me, some of the dressing rooms that you had when you first started playing. Did you ever have to dress in the basement or where they kept the liquor?

At Elmer’s, I dressed upstairs with the liquor bottles because they didn’t want blacks to come in. So I’d go upstairs and dress with the liquor bottles. That was our dressing room. It was on State Street.
I can relate to that. Did you play with Red Saunders? I think I read somewhere where you had a chance to perform at the same time Red Saunders…

Well, he’d give me some gigs you know. And I remember once, one of the ladies said, “Miss Donegan, you’re very democratic, you’re hiring a white man.” I said, “No, he’s been passing for colored for many years.” (laughs) You’re talking about Red Saunders, an oreo.
Yes. So, when did you leave the Chicago area? Did you go alone or with a band?
I left the Chicago area in 1944. I got a chance to do a picture with Cab Calloway called "Sensations of 45” and my mother went with me.
Where was that?
We went to Hollywood.
Did you go by plane, train?
We went by the Super Chief—it was a train, kind of exclusive you know.
Yes. Did they pay your way there?
Uh-huh. They paid our way there and gave me I think $3000 a week. Course I should have taken the MGM deal which was $750 for seven years.
Oh, what happened?
Well, the greedy manager took the three and the picture didn’t last but one and half weeks.
What was his name?
I call him Corkscrew Gervish.
Why did you call him Corkscrew Gervish?
Well, they say he was kind of crooked.
He was crooked, huh?
Yeah, he was crooked.
What percentage did he take during those times?
Well, they would always say they would take 10, but they always thought 10% of a dollar was 60 cents.
I remember.
It’s still that way. They take a commission off the top and one off the bottom.
When you arrived in Hollywood, did they put you in a special hotel, could you stay in the hotels or did they put you in a rooming house?
No, I stayed with the Shacklefords, someone’s personal home.
And you stayed there how long?
We stayed there about four or five weeks.
Do you have a print of the movie?

It’s easy to get. Eleanor Powell, Cab, Woody Herman and Sophie Tucker. It was a circus. And Gene Rodgers and I played against each other. He was a very good pianist. Cab was directing and shaking his hair.
He always shook his hair?
Oh yeah, sometimes it wouldn’t shake because he’d put some grease on it (both laugh).
Did you meet your first husband out there?

Yes, I met him in San Francisco. I met his sister first. I was going out with some of the AKA’s and so she introduced me to Helen Wright. Helen Wright wanted me to meet her brother. So I met him in San Francisco.
Was it love at first sight?
No. But as he gave me more things, I fell in love.
You fell in love or you fell in like?
Both. The more you give me, the more I like you (both laugh).
So was it a big wedding or did you get married at City Hall?
I took him down to City Hall. He was living in a place, so I moved in with him. You know, show women are always moving in with somebody.
Yes, that’s true. So, how long did you stay with this man?
We were together 15 years, off and on.
That’s amazing.
Yeah, for me. ‘Cause I get tired.
You stayed right in San Francisco all this time?
No, we lived in Los Angeles.
Can you tell me something—did he want to travel with you or did he try to make you stay home and miss gigs?
I don’t think he wanted to travel unless he had to, ‘cause he likes to stay around L.A. Whatever action he had before me, I guess he still kept.
What did he do for a living?
As little as possible.
So when you told him you were pregnant, what did he say?
“I didn’t tell you to have that brat.” I said, “Well, you got it.”
He didn’t want the baby?
Hmm-mm (no). But the “brat” is a genius.
A genius, eh? Did you have a very hard labor?
I thought so. Those nuns were pulling my hair, ‘cause I was about to climb off the table.
Pulling your hair?
Yeah, to make me get back on the table.
Dorothy, you were still performing. How long did it take you to have labor?
Oh, about eight hours or so.
That short.
Yeah
What did you say after you had that one?
I don’t want no more.
But you did, right?
One more. One bad one.
Well don’t…
He’d steal shortening out of gingerbread.
Steal shortening out of gingerbread? I’ll tell you, I’d like to know who was the second husband.
Oh my God, his name was Bill Miles and he was spoiled. He was a mama’s boy. So, he married me for my money and I married him for his. We both got fooled.
Really? So how long did you stay with this one and which one was the most handsome?
Both. I always went for handsome men and they usually no good. You should get somebody not so handsome. My mama said, “Why don’t you get somebody that likes you for a change?”
So, what did he do for a living?
Well, this one was into numbers. But he should have been writing them instead of booking them.
Too many people hit him?
Oh yeah. A lot of times he’d say they were hitting and they hadn’t.
Oh my goodness. So tell me, when you got your divorce, did you have to go to court then?
I went to court.
I imagine the judge really believed you, right?
No, he didn’t. He said, “She makes more money than you.” Men stick together usually.
You think that’s what happened?
Uh huh, ‘cause I could hardly get $10 a week alimony.
You mean the judge gave you $10 a week alimony?
Yeah, and then he didn’t pay it.
How about child support?
Nothing. I didn’t get nothing. I think his brother-in-law was a lawyer so he was able to do better than me.
Yes. How about the third husband?
The third husband was around 80 years old. He owned a lot of property.
Was he more your mental equal?
No, I thought he had more money than he did. He had to pay his wife $700 a month. I just married him ‘cause I didn’t have any gigs.
I can understand. Whenever you would not have gigs, you would get restless.
Or to get married.
You would get married, not restless.
Well, I guess that’s a form of restlessness.
Yes. Could you tell me, who kept your children while you were on the road?
All different people.
Like who?
My mother, some cousins. But I found out, if you’re going to have children, you should keep them yourself.
Amen. So, the children, when you came off the road, were they glad to see you or were they resentful?
They were glad.
They were glad.
And John T’s son was staying with the Wrights, they were very wealthy, his brother- in-law and sister-in-law, the ones who introduced John T to me. He went to school with the Jacksons, you know.
When you had to leave them, how did you feel?
Very bad. ‘Cause they didn’t deserve that. I shouldn’t have had no children.
You’re almost like a split person.
You can’t be in two places at the same time.
But you want to.
You have to earn a living if you don’t have a husband.

Yes. I know a lot of show women have this same major problem, even now, that was not just the ‘40’s. So, how did you resolve it? When they had their high school prom and graduation, did you go to their graduation?
Well, a lot of times I’d be away when they were graduating. And the second child, I don’t remember him graduating. When he got 18, they threw him out of high school.
But I tell you, did you kind of have a family on the road when ….
They’d go on the road with me. The young one went with me to Yugoslavia. And he acted so bad, they said, “Either you go or he goes.”
Is that so?
Uh-huh. And he went back to America from Yugoslavia, he was just that smart.
Did you make a family out of the musicians and the dancers while you were performing?
I don’t think so.
You were just a loner?
Yeah. You play and go home.
Did you have a hobby on the road?
No.
What did you do when you went back to your hotel?
Nothing.
Sleep?
Yeah, I’m a sleeper.
You didn’t like to play cards or anything like that?
Uh-uhh.
But your folks did. Didn’t your father like to play cards?
Yeah, he liked to play cards. He’d hit the cards…”Hit the cards, Dummy…(you) don’t beat it unless you got some aces.” Things like that.
‘Cause I remember, my folks were the same way, they liked to play cards. Dirty Hearts?
Oh, I love Dirty Hearts.
I knew you liked to play cards. Dirty Hearts, right?
Mm-hmmm. Bridge, too.
Bridge, yes. Are you a good bridge player?
I’m not using a book you know. I’m not using Culbertson or Scheinwold, but I guess sometimes I’m lucky and win.
Did you have a favorite color to wear on stage?
I like black.
Really?
Mm-hmmm.
Dramatic.
It shows my skin tone better.
I agree. In fact, the first time I saw you, you had on black.
Yeah, I always had on a black dress.
Did you find it hard to get your clothes cleaned properly on the road?
Yeah, you have to take them back to New York or Chicago or L.A.
So that meant you had to have a lot of clothes.
That’s right, ‘cause they’d get funky.
So, did you figure out how to wear your clothes to advantage, in other words, did you have tops and bottoms that you changed around or did you have just one-piece dresses?
I had two pieces, and one pieces.
Did you wash your own laundry in the hotel room?
Yeah, I didn’t have nothing to wash but bloomers.
That’s correct.
That’s it.
Yes. Did you carry those little clothespins?
No, I just put them on the top of the bathtub.
And let them dry.
Mm-hmm.
I’d like to have you tell us a little more about your grandparents and where your roots came from.

Well, my grandmother was an Indian and she had 13 children by my grandfather. He was a rascal. He was Irish. And she was very angry at him. He had had a baby by her sister. She missed him, though. She shot him.
She shot him?
Yeah, but she didn’t hit him.
Oh (laughs). Where were they living?
In Newton, Mississippi.
Newton, Mississippi. How close was that to Birmingham?
I don’t know but it’s close to Jackson, Mississippi. Where are you from, Birmingham?
All my people are from Birmingham.
Oh, that’s good. Well, you got to be from someplace.
So where was your mother and father from?
Mother was from Newton. She was pretty. And my father was from Huntsville, Alabama. He was a chef cook.
What were their names?
Mother’s name was Ella Baker Day. My father was Donazell Hogan Donegan.
And, how about your grandparents’ names?
My grandmother was named Veenie Day, she was a Willis, I think. And her husband was Matt Day.
So, what did your mother do for a living?
She probably did domestic work. She used to work for the Jones Brothers.
Oh.
You heard of them?
Yeah, they’re from Buffalo, New York.
Oh I didn’t know that.
Yes.
I think they paid her $3 a day. They handled the numbers back in Chicago.
So, what did your grandfather do other than make children?
Make children, I guess. He didn’t do much.
Did you have a farm or how did they make a living?
I don’t know. But they made it.
Do you look like them?
No, he was very light, or white, yeah. And my grandmother was very, very dark, like a Indian. That’s the way the white man and the colored woman are free.
How about your brother?
My brother was nice-looking. He died about six years ago.
What was his name?
Leon.
Was he younger?
Younger. And he drank a lot of whiskey.
Ohhh. Did you have to babysit him?
No. I told him there were three shifts making it.
So, you never had to babysit him.
No.
What did you do at home, other than practice?
Joe Williams said that’s all I did. Joe Williams lived in the next building, you know. And he would sell newspapers on the corner.
Joe Williams, the blues singer?
Yeah. He said, “That broad, all she did was practice.”
How old was he when you knew him?
He was about 18.
And how old were you at the time?
I was much younger. I’d be about 12 or 13.
And what was he doing musically at that time?
Well, he was in the hospital sometimes you know. I don’t want to tell it. But we know about it, don’t we? He’d be selling newspapers sometimes.
When you performed in Chicago, can you remember the very first nightclub you performed?
I think I worked either the 65 Club or the Day Swingland (?)
Where was that located?
On 55th Street.
Was that near Cottage Grove?
No, it was near South Park.
Did you have a cover charge, or people just came in?
They just came in.
Did they have a regular show or were you the main act?
I wasn’t the main act, but they let me play.
Did they have a dancer and MC? In those days, sometimes, they’d have an MC, a shake dancer, a comedian, then the musicians?
Something like that.
That’s what they had for you?
Yes.
A complete show?
Yes.
Do you remember how much a shot of whiskey was?
No, not really. Willie Bigtop says, there’s 20 shots in a bottle.
It’s true.
Can you tell me a little more about your father. You said he was a chef cook. Can you tell me a little bit more about what he did?

Well, he was a chef cook on the Burlington Quincy Railroad. And he’d bring us turkeys home, cooked in a cheesecloth. He could really bake. And he used to come home and play cards. And my mother, when he would come home, she would pretend like she did a lot of work. She always married railroad men because she said they were gone all the time. But, she would be pretending she’s busy and then when he’d leave, she’d do what she wanted to do. I like that.
Was he gone much of the time?
Yes. She didn’t marry a man unless he stayed gone all the time. They must stay gone.
And did you just have one brother or did you have other siblings?
One brother, Leon. He was an engineer. And he was sort of lazy.
How about other extended family that might have gone up to Chicago? Did your mother and father have sisters or brothers that also migrated to Chicago about the same time?
Yeah, a lot of people changed trains in Chicago. They came from the South, you know. And, they liked to come to Chicago. They wanted to get away from the prejudice down there.
What part of town did they live in?
We lived on the South Side. 47th Street. 4738 St. Lawrence.
And where in your neighborhood, where would music be played?

On 42nd Street. We’d play at the DeLisa, and we played at the Allstars. And then there was the Grand Terrace where Earl Hines played. Then there were some sewers around 47th Street where Dan Grissom played and Howlin’ Wolf, and people like that would play.
How about theatres?
The Rio Theatre, and the Oriental Theatre and the Dump. That was on 47th Street.
Tell me about the Dump. I haven’t heard of that one.
That was where Cleo Brown played. And I got a chance to hear her. I liked her very much.
Do you remember the first time you saw Cleo Brown? What year was it?

Oh, that was about, I must have been about 14 or 15. She could really play boogie­ woogie. And she had a style where she could roll the bass. She played a number called “The Stuff is Here” and I went home and practiced it and learned it.
Tell me more about Cleo Brown’s playing. We don’t know a whole lot about her these days.

No, she wasn’t well known, but she could really play. She had a good right hand a good left hand (demonstrates while singing the notes). And in this left hand, the notes would be buzzing. She could make them buzz. I like the way she played. She wasn’t classical, like I, but I liked what I heard.
Tell me about, you mentioned Howlin’ Wolf, I think he might have come a little later. Tell me about some of the musical influences that were taking place in Chicago.

They were hollerin’ the blues and then there was Dan Grissom, he could really sing, you know. And then, Muddy Waters, and let’s see, Memphis Slim. You would hear these people play in these sewers and I’d go in and see them, you know. They say, “What would you like?” I’d say, “Some champagne” and they would buy me champagne and I’d listen to them.
Let’s stick on Memphis Slim for a second. Was his music considered in the community to be less sophisticated than some of the other piano players?
I guess so because people didn’t understand it as well as they… he made most of his money in Europe, though.
Yeah, that was later.
Yes, he loved my playing a lot.

Let’s go back to your musical training. You mentioned two of your teachers. From what I’ve read, you started to play at six and by eight you were taking classical lessons. Let’s start when you were six. What were the first things you gravitated to on the piano?

I like classical music you know. Because there was probably more barriers against you learning classical. I would learn Bach, Beethoven, Czerny, Hanon, you name it. Then I went downtown and studied after I had exhausted Professor Sims.
Professor Sims was your first or second teacher?
Yes.
Which one, first or second?
First.
How did Professor Sims teach you? What kind of exercises or techniques or reading…
Oh, he’d teach me Bach and then I would learn pieces like Rondo Capriccioso by Mendelssohn. And things like that.
How quickly would you pick up music, was it something you just digested?
Yes, it was like a duck in water. If you can hear it, you can play it. That’s what Art Tatum said. You first got to hear it and then you can play it. You got to have an ear.
How about some of the other teachers you had as a child?
I had Lillian Brown, very good teacher. She taught me the Wallin’ Hop (?), things like that. Mendelssohn Concerto.
Were your parents supportive of you playing classical music?
Oh yes, they liked for me to play it. They liked for me to play and bring the money home. And whatever brought it home, they liked it.
What were your parents’ musical preferences? What were their favorite kinds of music?
Well, they didn’t care long as it had feeling. They said, “You must have feeling with this music.”
Did either of them play instruments?
No. My father had tried to play a trumpet but he never learned.
And your mother?
She was just pretty.
Who did you get to see play music as a child? Who were your musical role models?

I used to see Fats Waller and Earl Hines. And I used to hear him play at the Grand Terrace (sings). He would tingle the piano all night. Raymond Walters, he was a Tatum protégée. But everybody in Chicago could play I think.
Now, you had a piano in your home?
Yes, we bought one for $50.
Was that before you started playing or as a result of your playing?
Before.
How about any neighbors or extended family members? Did anyone else close to home show you or take you under their wing as a young child?
No. Hannah and Clemente, Kramer…]
I’d like to know—what do you use to warm yourself up and get your fingers ready to play when you haven’t played for a while?
Oh, Czerny, a lot of Czerny and a lot of Hanon, the Italian version of Hanon.
Yes.
I use the Brahms exercises.
Could you explain a little bit how Hanon affects your fourth and fifth fingers? That’s the weakest fingers on both hands.
It is, and you just have to practice it until you get tired and hold the others down. But these two, you have to use them a lot.
Because they’re only on one ligament.
Oh, is that it?
The rest of them have their own separate but these two, that’s why they’re so weak.
The pinky and ring finger.
I used to catch a fifty-dollar bill with that ring finger.
Did you? Really?
Tell me about records in the home? What records sounded good to you, who would bring them home and ….

Well, I used to hear Gene Austin (sings—“what makes the world go round…”). Let’s see, what else did we listen to? Our father loved Lunceford. He didn’t like Duke so much. But he loved Lunceford, he said he jumped, you know. And Martha Davis, I met. She was talking about Art Tatum. He was very good. He’s my idol. I think he’s every pianist’s idol.
Were there any Tatum records in the Donegan household?

Oh, yeah. I had to hide them because these musicians will steal them. I met him when I was 18 through Rozelle Gayle, did you know him? Rozelle was a giant and he had a tongue that’d reach from here to here, and he could make it quiver. But he could play like Art Tatum and sing like Caruso. And Tatum would say, “I don’t know what to do about that girl. They say she made Art Tatum practice and Hazel Scott leave the country.”
Did you have any real close friends when you were coming up?
Yeah, like Pauline Willis was a close friend. Let’s see, who else? A few…I think she was it. We would argue but we stayed friends.
You mentioned baseball just in passing.

Well, I used to play baseball with the fellows. And I could hit the ball over the fence. But I decided I was going to hurt my fingers so I had to quit. I used to play with Charlie Carpenter’s brother, Richard Carpenter. Charlie used to handle Earl Hines.
Tell me about your personality as a child. Did you keep to yourself, were you causing trouble, were you a good student?
I was a pretty good student. I was temperamental though. I admit that. Now I’m less temperamental, but I still call it like I see it. Two and two got to make four.
How about radio when you were coming up. You mentioned Earl Hines’ broadcasts.
I used to listen to Amos and Andy, and people like that, you know, coming up. And Mert and Marge, Bing Crosby, Jack Benny, people like that.
Were there any musical styles you heard through radio that you had not been familiar with before?
I used to like Alec Templeton who had stolen some of Art Tatum’s runs. Carmen Carvallero I liked. He was very good. Earl Hines.
Tell me about this broadcast from the Grand Terrace.
He used to play, you could hear him in the alley. “Fatha’ Hines, Fatha’ Hines.” So I would try to mimic him.
And how old were you at the time?
Let’s go back to the musical training. I guess by the time you were 10 you were playing organ in the church.
I didn’t play organ long because they wouldn’t pay me. And if you play organ, you can’t play piano.
How is that, explain it to me.

Well, it’s a different touch. If you play piano, you can’t play organ. If you play organ, you can’t play piano. The touch is much different. One is a hard touch and the other’s a delicate touch. It’s hard to separate the two touches. So I said, “Oh, I better play piano.” Because you can change the sound of the organ with one button.
Tell me about church—which church did you attend as a child?
Episcopal Church. Another one was Reverend Bolton’s church.
What denomination was that?
Baptist.
Was your mom of one denomination and your father of another?
No, my father didn’t go. He thought the church would fall in on him. My mother would go to St. Mark’s Episcopal Church and she stuck to that.
Was she brought up Episcopal in Mississippi?
No, but she liked to go to Reverend Redman’s church.
And which was that?
Episcopal.
And what about the Baptist Church, how did that fall in?
I didn’t stick with that too long. We were Episcopalians.
Were you playing music in both the Episcopal Church and the Baptist Church?
Sometimes.
Can you tell me how the music differed between the two denominations.
In the Baptist Church it’s more bluesy. The Episcopalian Church is more staid and relaxed.
When you were playing organ was that in the Episcopal or the Baptist Church or both?
The Baptist Church, but I quit after two or three weeks.
Let’s just talk about the influence of gospel music and particularly with Thomas Dorsey being in Chicago at the time you were coming up. How did that work its way into the Dorothy Donegan style?

Well, if you listen to him, some of it’s got to rub off. People like Willie Webb and Robert Mays could do that better than me. But I could sneak it in pretty good. But they could beat me playing it. There are certain gospel chords. Like Mahalia Jackson had an accompanist named Mildred Falls. She can really play that gospel piano.
Was there anything in the gospel piano sound or style that really appealed to you or did you just prefer to stick to the jazz and the classical training?
I think I’d rather stick to mine and they stick to theirs. But I still sneak some of it in.
Can you tell me technically what that gospel sound is? What are the gospel chords or rhythmically, can you describe…?
It’s a C7, F7 and G7 back to the C7.
How does that differ from a blues piano style using the same chords, in either feel, rhythmically, melodically, can you just describe that difference?
I think the feel in the same you know, but the gospel has more meaning. When you hear it, you arise to it. And the blues, they have their thing too.
Between the ages of 10 and 14, from what I gather, you’d become a professional musician around the age of 14?
Yes.
What school did you graduate from?
DuSable.
Oh, DuSable. You had a famous teacher there. Captain Dyette. Tell us about this man, I’ve heard so much about him.
He’d cuss you out…I loved him, but he’d call you a MF in a minute.
He would? But you had to do the right thing, right?
“That’s a Bb7!” And he’d cuss you out if you made a mistake.
He must have been a wonderful teacher.
Oh, he was great, yeah.
Somebody really should do a life story on this man. Because he was behind so many great musicians.
Tommy Rigsby.
Name some more.
Redd Foxx, saxophone player, Gene Ammons. And he always would get the students out of jail.
Dickie Morris.
Dickie Morris.
Did you go to your high school prom?
I played for it. Yeah, I earned that dollar, two dollars.
Made the money on the prom, right?
Yeah, well, he would give you money to play the High Jinx. And if the principal got jealous, (he) stopped it.
There’s always somebody, right?
There’s always a- holes.
Tell me one more thing. Did you ever think that you would give up your music for romance?
No.
Never even for a minute?
No, I’d have to be hurt. And so I said, “Well, if I give up everything, he’ll just be with another woman. So I’ll just buy a dress and get over him.”
Did you ever think about going to college?
I went to college.
Where did you go?
I went to LACC and UCLA, USC.
What did you take?
Music and Sociology.
What was attractive about Sociology?
They think all musicians are stupid. So I said—where’d you go to school? Oh, USC. Where’d you study at…
Did you like the classes?
I like to be a student anyway. And then I got two doctorates.
They were bestowed upon you?
Yes.
Where from?
University of Maryland Eastern Shore and Roosevelt. But I’m always at somebody’s university.
Who did you think was the best woman pianist?
Besides myself?
Besides yourself.
I liked Laura Crosby.
I never heard of Laura Crosby. Tell us about her.
She was a little heavy, I’d have to watch out.
Where’s she from?
Chicago.
About the same time you were growing up?
Yes.
Did she ever record?
I don’t think so but she had a beautiful touch. She didn’t have my fire and everything but she was great.
Was she born in Chicago?
Yes, she was Israel Crosby’s sister.
Boy, that is news! Is she still alive?
Did she sing as well?
Great pianist.
That’s very different. Because most of the time they make women have to perform to get your money. I must say that is true.
She didn’t make much money but she was good.
Do you remember some of the nightclubs she played at?
She played at all the sewers like I. Played the Allstars and dumps like that.
She played the sewers?
I did too. That’s how you learn.
That’s true, the Bucket O’ Blood.
Bucket O’ Blood, the Pioneer Lounge. Laura could really play.
What did you think of Mary Lou Williams?
As a woman or pianist?
Is there any difference? I think maybe we’ll just stick to the music.
She was a great pianist to accompany a band. I didn’t like her as a soloist.
‘Cause there is a difference.
She didn’t excite me playing solo. Now, she could swing a band.
She could swing a band. And good writer, good arranger.
And she and Hazel Scott were good friends. Did you know Hazel Scott?
Yes.
Oh, you met her?
I met her in Akron, OH.
Imagine that. She used to come in, she and Mary Lou, and they’d talk while I was playing.
Now, that’s an insult. Oh, sorry about that.
So I said, “Come on up here, you two B’s.”
You didn’t tell them that.
Yes I did.
Did they come up?
No, they ran out.
Of course.
They would make noise while you’re playing.
That’s not very nice. But you really respected Mary Lou as a musician?
Yes, as a writer. And she could accompany a band. She could swing a band.
Is there anybody else you knew that had the facility. Sometimes, it’s not chops but feeling and could move a room.
Basil Spears maybe, did you know her?
No
She could play.
You’re calling people that we’d like to find out more about. Was she from Chicago?
Out of New York. And Hazel Scott was a good entertainer. She looked beautiful at the piano.
True. White dress and all.
And she could show her bust and move the whole room.
Yes.
She had that going.
Could you tell us the difference between Chicago players and New York players?
I think Chicago players had more balls.
Even the ladies?
We had more balls than the New York.
How were they different?
In the playing. I think they knew more music than the New York—the New York people didn’t play with any left hand. We had to play with left hand because Buck and Bubbles told us we had to.
Is that why, wait a minute…
Buck and Bubbles. He’d say, “What you doing with your left hand, you leave it in the dressing room?”
Were the Chicago musicians more percussive?
Maybe so.
Why would you think that? I’ve found it to be true too, but I just want to know what you think.
Well, it was cold back then, I guess they had to play harder to get the gigs, you know.
Perhaps, but do you find the New York musicians were more…
Timid?
They seem to be more flowery, they’d play a lot of runs and…
Clyde Hart, and people like that, did you know him?
No I did not.
Clyde Hart. And Herman Chittison.
Yes.
He could play. But he wasn’t heavy as the Chicago cats. And then there was Gideon Honore.
Where was he from?
Chicago. Those Chicago cats could play. Bill Huff, Rozelle Gayle. They could stride, too.
Yes. Well, you know they had some New York stride pianists also.
Like who?
Lucky Roberts.
Oh yeah, he could play, he was really heavy on that piano.
Didn’t he play in New York?
He had his own club.
Didn’t you have your own club also?
I had mine in Los Angeles on 45th and Western.
Tell us about that venture.
Me and my ex-husband. He didn’t want to pay me and then he wanted to go with every girl in the joint.
But what made you decide to have a club. That to me is the epitome of a monument to oneself.
He wanted a club. Everybody likes attention. Then when they get the bills, they don’t want to pay them.
Did you play in there every night?
Yeah, he made me play, even when I was having a baby.
How long did it last?
It didn’t last too long ‘cause I said, “I ain’t going to play unless you pay me. You can go with everybody in here but you must pay me.”
I don’t blame you. So, what was the name of it?
The Morocco. It was pretty. And then his sister and brother-in-law were giving us the money to front it, you know.
Do you have any pictures of the club?
I think my ex-husband has a picture of it.
I’ll bet it was beautiful.
Oh, and the food was good. We should have stuck together. I should have played free and let him go with all the women. Sometimes you have to do that.
I’d like to hear about that club. For a woman to have a club like that.
It was gorgeous. And people like Doris Duke came in. And Groucho Marx. He says, “Oh, you ain’t drawing, these women are drawing” I said, “You’ll see.” But it was great.
Who would handle the business end? Was that your ex-husband or were you involved in that as well?
He didn’t want me to handle none of the money. He had his sisters handle it. Everything he had, he had in his peoples’ name. If he moved to a woman’s house, he’d only take his toothbrush.
How about the booking, was that also his sisters?
Yeah, they are a closely knit family.
Was it unusual to have women in the business of clubs?
No, not necessarily. Because Dorothy Brandon had a club. And Maurice used to cook at the Dunbar. But he wanted his sisters to handle his money.
Who were some of the acts, the talent, that were booked into the club?
He’d have some jive organist play. And then he’d have Wild Bill Davis.
Was it musicians that would be competing with you for gigs? Different style?
Not necessarily.
What were some of the popular styles of music that would be represented in the club?
Well, they’d just have to play funky. Make you jump. Starting on the F7 . . . And the Bb7.
What year did it open?
And how long did it survive?
Just a year. But if I’d taken over, it would have survived more.
You mentioned that your ex-husband made you perform while you were pregnant. Was that common for women musicians or was that unusual?
That was common. Because the men thought the money should go on. It was like a pregnant prostitute out of business, the woman stopped working.

Tell me about performing while you’re pregnant. Obviously the movie that you did would not have been a possibility if you were pregnant. But was it expected for women to hide their pregnancy as well as possible?
Not necessarily. But to perform, yes. To keep going as if it didn’t happen.
How long after giving birth and recovering from the pregnancy would it take before you would return to performing?
About three or four weeks.
And is that typical of other woman musicians?
Yeah, like Martha Davis performed while she was pregnant. Did you know her?
Yes.
She was a great musician too.

You were mentioning a few minutes ago some of the other women musicians whose names we didn’t know. Are there any others? One of the reasons we do this is to find out who we don’t know about, who didn’t get a chance to record that were also influential either in the community in the music scene. Are there any others you can recall?
Was Camille Howard a piano player or a singer? Well, Camille Howard was with Roy Milton. Annie Laurie. Hadda Brooks.
Were these primarily pianists?
And singers. Nellie Lutcher.
What format were most of these women performing in? Were they performing in trios, were they performing solo piano, in dance bands, what was the most common format?
Some of them performed by themselves and some of them performed with a trio.
Tell me about the popularity of the trio format.
As opposed to what?
As opposed to playing solo?
With a trio you can rest more. And when you’re playing by yourself, you got to do it all.
Let’s talk about Nat Cole. To what extent was he the reason for the popularity of the piano trio?

He was so good, I think. And he had taste. And he was a protégé of Earl Hines. And his wife wanted him to fire his quartet. So he became a trio and started singing alone with the trio in the background.
Tell me about Nat Cole in Chicago when you were coming up.

Well, he used to play with brown-skinned models and he and his wife were on the road. And he used to have a band and he used to play at the Warwick Hall. They were very good. He played the piano with one finger. But it was tasty what he left out. And so he became a super star.
Tell me about the whole Earl Hines/Nat Cole lineage. Tell me what Nat’s playing that Earl Hines is not and just the relationship between the two players.

Well, Nat studied--didn’t study, copied—all of Earl Hines’ licks. So he put them in with his and that became the Nat Cole sound. And then he started singing which made it better. That rounded it out. (Starts singing, “Straighten Up and Fly Right”). And his wife would write these catchy ditties—Nadine. And they were going pretty good before he quit her, you know.
How influential was Nat Cole in Chicago? Was he known by everybody, was everyone trying to copy Nat Cole and his popularity, or were people pursuing their own direction?
People were pursuing their own directions. And everybody, they weren’t bowled over, but they liked him.
How about the boogie-woogie craze?

Albert Ammons, Meade Lux Lewis—oh, they could really play. Two hands, you know they played two pianos. They went to New York and played at Café Society. Two fat men at the piano, they could really play boogie-woogie all. You have to have endurance and persistence to play that long. Pete Johnson, that completes it.
Pete was a pianist, the rest of them are boogie-woogie players.
Albert, too.
When did boogie-woogie really start to become popular? The recording started in 1938 with Ammons and Lewis.
I guess it started in the ‘40’s.
How big a development was that, specifically in Chicago?
I guess it was… it didn’t go crazy like Elvis Presley.
Was boogie-woogie more popular in New York?
Possibly.
How about where it would be booked in Chicago nightclubs?
There were some clubs downtown where it would be booked.
Such as?
Where Chuck Palm works. I forgot the name of it.

Could you talk a little bit about the different clubs in Chicago and the different kinds of music they would book? Was one club, for instance, known for booking boogie-woogie as opposed to a smoother, more refined sound? And specifically, were the clubs that booked more sophisticated music in a certain part of town; could you comment on that?

Yes. There was the Capital Lounge, the used to book Maurice Rocco, and he was a boogie-woogie pianist. He used to play standing up. Brass Rail. And the clubs all on the north side. They had a lot of clubs out there but I can’t think of them now.
The first club you played at was…
The Garrick Stage Bar.
They also had the High Jinx listed…
The High Jinx was a school play.
Tell me more about that…
Captain Dyette would take all the talent and book it on one day. And it was successful. And it was called the High Jinx. It would go two or three days.
So, it’s more of a school talent and music program.
Yes. It was as good as anything downtown was.
Was that done every year?
Yes, until this old principal, Chauncy Woods, stopped it.
Now, were you getting paid for playing the High Jinx?
Yeah, you’d get a dollar a night, which was good money then.
Was it held at the school itself?
Yes.
Was it attended by students and parents and the community?
Everybody. It was packed.
Big event.
Mm-hmm.
Now you obviously were playing piano. Were you doing classical repertoire or jazz or a combination of the two?
Both. Everything.
And that was your first paid gig I suppose.
No, I had done some sewers before that for a buck and one gig I worked, I got only a quarter, ‘cause the broad said I had eaten three hot dogs. So, it’s 35 cents for three, so the quarter was my pay.
Now, you mention the sewers, the clubs. Do you remember the names of any of them?
[End of first CD]
Like, the Silhouette, The Capital Lounge, Elmer’s, The Brass Rail, The Bar Music, places like that.

I wanted to ask you about competitiveness between musicians, especially as a teenager before your professional career really gets rolling—cutting contests or opportunities to compete with other musicians and learn from other musicians. Could you comment on that?

Musicians had cutting contests. You get in there and you got to show what you can do. So I’m going for the jugular. A lot of times I’d win. Like, Art Tatum had a cutting contest with Hazel Scott and Erroll Garner. So they got smart with him one day. And Hazel Scott got smart and so on. He played so much piano, ‘til she ran off screaming. And then he played so much piano for Erroll Garner, ‘til he played “Little Man, You’ve Had a Busy Day.” And he ain’t been back since.
According to my notes, and I want you to correct me if I’m wrong, you’re playing the High Jinx event around the age of 14?
Yeah.
So that would place it about 1936 or so. Getting a dollar a night. Who were some of the other performers, students I assume?
Savannah Strong, Tommy Rigsby, Bert McCloskey, you know all local people. But they were very good.
Were they students as well?
Yeah, students but they had talent. And then a girl named Squeaky. She could really sing.
So, singers, and what other kinds of entertainers?
Dancers, Raymond Sneed—he could dance, he was in “Stormy Weather.”
I know Ray Sneed, he choreographed an act for us in New York City. He used to dance the tree. He would become a tree and leaves would come out and branches come out. Did you play for him?
In the High Jinx, yes. Of course I was with the band.
You were with the band, but did you also perform solo?
Yes.
Tell me about some of the acts that you would accompany.
Ray Sneed and Squeaky and Savannah Strong.
How big was the band?
About 10 or 12 pieces.
How would they get arrangements?
Captain Dyette would arrange it.
I have in my notes that at the age of 15, about 1937, you started playing Garrick Stage Bar. Can you tell us about that?

He was a pugilist and he used to train fighters, and so he hired me and Billie Holiday. He booked her, he thought she was a boy. And Red Saunders. Not Red Saunders, Red Allen. And Lips Page, he’d hire all the best talent. Joe Glaser would let him hire them real cheap. And I played down there. And then he decided to put me in a concert. So he put me in a concert and I sold it out.
Now, “he” being Joe Glaser, or ….
Joe Sherman, who worked for Joe Glaser. And he had beat up Lips Page. He hit him in the mouth. So we got a free vacation that week.
When did Joe Sherman come into your life. Was he your first manager?
No, he was not a manager. But he wanted to put me in a concert opposite Vladimir Horowitz. And so I outsold Horowitz.
At the age of 17.
I had 500 more people. And he hit me on the butt and said, “Go on out there and lead with your left.”
Tell me about the money at Garrick Stage Bar.
Oh, I got $250 a week, which was a lot of money.
Was there anything that came between playing the High Jinx at the age of 16 and playing the Garrick Stage Bar at the age of 17?
Incidental gigs, you know. Nothing big. But he took me from Elmer’s and brought me around the corner for $250 a week.

I have Elmer’s being a little bit later, 1942 but I want you to lay this out. I know to distrust the liner notes. I do want to attempt to get an accurate chronology. So, at the age of 17, Garrick Stage Bar, does that sound right? $250 a week, there? So, that’s your first real money.
Yes and then I went upstairs. After the concert, He didn’t want to raise me so I went across the street to the Latin Quarter. For $750.
Was this before or after you made the recordings for Bluebird?
After.

The information I have suggests that the big money came a little bit later. I could be wrong here but I’ve got Garrick Stage Bar in, you would be 17 years old in 1939. And then the Allstars, that would have been about 1940.
That’s a dump, yeah.
So, you wouldn’t have been making the big money before ….
Was that per night?
Yes.
How many nights a week would you play?
One or two.
I think something that comes between this point in your career and making the big money is playing with Bob Tinsley’s band at The Swingland.
That was before.
Before the big money.
Mm-hmm.
Tell me about Bob Tinsley, the band—I gather this was a dance orchestra?
Yes.
How did it differ playing with a band than playing solo or in a trio?
I don’t think I liked it too much but I took it anyway.
How big was the band?
About six or seven pieces.
What kind of repertoire would they perform?
All square music, you know. “One O’ Clock Jump” or something like that.
And other than The Swingland, where would they play?
I don’t know of any other place. They weren’t popular.
How much money were they taking in, in a night? What would be your salary playing with…
Two or three bucks.
Back at this time as a teenager and young adult, late teen years, were you still living at home?
Yes
Would you have to give your mother some of the money or all of the money?
Some of it, I’d give her some of it and keep some of it.
Although this is before you had your first big money, you were earning a living or helping…
Yeah, she wanted ten bucks a week. For room and board.
Were you able to pay that from your earnings?
Yeah, I’d get tips.
What would be a common tip?
Five, ten and one man gave us a dollar once. So I said, “Is this going three ways?”
How were tips divided?
It depends on my mood.
With someone like Bob Tinsley leading the band, would he take a larger percentage?
No, not if it got in my hands.
After that, Costello’s Grill?
That was before then.
Before Bob Tinsley.
That was at the beginning of my career.
Was that a solo gig?
Solo.
How did you get booked into that?
Some of my mother’s friend’s boy told the man downstairs about me.
And as a result…
I got the gig.
Any sense of how much money you would get for that?
$60 a week.
$60 a week. Is that the first big money?
Yeah.
Where was Costello’s Grill located?
On North Dearborn. Downtown.
Different part of town than you’d been playing.
Yeah. ‘Cause there was a segregated union and they didn’t want the acts to play downtown.
So, did that cause problems for you?
Uh-uhh. They can’t tell me where to work. They didn’t get the job.
Were other African-Americans playing downtown at this time?
No.
How about transportation downtown from the South Side
I’d take the L.
Were there places you were not supposed to go…
With segregation?
With the segregation, Jim Crow, was it safe for you to travel from the South Side to Costello’s Grill?
Yeah.
How did performing solo at Costello’s Grill differ from some of the venues that you had played previously?
It was just another gig. I could play anywhere.
Did it give you more freedom, being able to play whatever you wanted?
Yeah, well, I could always play what I wanted.
Was it more work because you were playing by yourself?
I didn’t realize it at the time. I guess I had more energy.
What elements of the Dorothy Donegan style that we’re familiar with today were in place back in 1939, 1940?
I don’t know. I know I had a good left hand, that helped me a lot.
Weren’t you mixing your music from classical to jazz to boogie, even during that time?
Yeah, I could swing the classics, you know.
That was sort of like a trademark with you.
Yeah, me and Hazel…
You and Hazel Scott…
She was the Dorothy Donegan of New York. And I was doing the same thing. She had a ceiling on my development, though.
What do you mean?
Well, she had New York sewed up.
Why do you say that?
Well, the first one who gets it, gets it. And she went to Europe and that’s when I got a better hold. Then they cussed out Lady Bird, and Lady Bird did this (loud noise).
Oh yeah.

You remember that? They wanted her to resign from the D.A.R. and she said, “I don’t give a darn (unintelligible).” So her husband called her the “last lady of the land.” So that finished her in America. So that let me go to New York.
Did you ever meet Mabel Mercer?
Oh yeah. Who hasn’t?
Did you ever play for her?
No, I’d go see her with some of my friends. Did you know her?
Yes, through Jo Jones.
Oh, did Jo know her too?
Yes.
She was stuffy.
Well, that was like New York style. That’s the difference you were talking about between Chicago….
(sings) “It was just one of those things…”
Chicago had blood and muscles.
And grits.
And energy. Where did you play in New York City?
The Embers.
Miss Donegan, can you tell me about Hillard Brown’s band?
Yeah, I used to play with him. We used to play at the Allstars for $15 a week.
$15 for the whole band or for you?
For me.
And was that before or after Costello’s?
After. And then the man would hold his hand up and that means you could go home. I often played all night.
Let me step back from Hillard Brown just for a second. If you were making $60 a week at Costello’s Grill, how did that gig come to an end, why did that fall apart?
I don’t know. Maybe I said something smart.
Were you known for saying something smart?
Yeah.
Would that get you in trouble frequently?
Yeah. Some things are safer unsaid.
How did Hillard Brown’s band differ from Bob Tinsley’s?
I think Hillard was a better musician than Bob Tinsley.
You were still playing at the Allstars which you considered not to be one of the finer clubs of Chicago.
That’s how you learn how to play is play those sewers.
I also have listed that Hillard Brown’s band was performing at The Tank.
That’s where we performed, for Adolf. And he would raise his hand, “Now you can go home, thanks a lot.”
He was the owner of the club?
Yes.
And his name was…
Adolf.
Adolf? What part of town was The Tank in?
McCormick and Pratt Blvd., on the North Side of Chicago.
Any major differences between North Side and the South Side clubs you described earlier?
No colored came in.
Why is that?
They didn’t want ‘em.
Further musical training…Chicago Conservatory. When did that come about for you?
Ruth Brown. Then I went to Chicago Musical College and studied with a Rudolph Ganz. And then I went out to California and started going to USC.
How long were you at the Chicago Conservatory?
About a year.
And what were you studying in particular?
Mendelssohn and Gershwin preludes.

Your decision to further your musical studies, in particular your classical musical studies…how was that reflected in the kinds of gigs you were getting with Hillard Brown, the solo gig at Costello’s Grill, the performances with Bob Tinsley. Tell me about your desire to play classical music versus jazz. Was there room for you to play both?
There was room for me to play both. In classical, you’ve got to fill the halls, though. But I’d rather play classical. I think classical stimulates me and the jazz pays me.
Tell me about “classical stimulates me.” What is it about the music?
I like to hear Ashkenazy and Horowitz and all the great masters play. I don’t practice jazz at home. But I love to hear classical masters play.
Has your technique with classical repertoire ever been such that you are at that level, the classical master?
Not quite. But I have played with the symphonies. But I said, “Oooohh, Horowitz….”
To become a classical master, would you have had to give up the jazz influence?
I think so. That’s all you do. You don’t have no man, no woman, no nothing.
Did you ever have the desire to give up jazz and pursue classical music exclusively?
Sometimes.
Was there ever a particular time that you were close, can you elaborate on that?
Yeah, I was close but you still have to pay your bills.
Was there a time that you were close to giving up jazz to pursue classical?
Yeah.
What happened?
Some bills came.
Does jazz pay the bills?
Yes, classical don’t pay them.
What led you to leave the Chicago Conservatory and go to the Chicago Musical College?
I heard, you always hear about better teachers. So, I’m always curious. So I go see what’s out there.
Did you give up performing in the clubs at this time or were you studying by day and playing jazz by night?
Both.
Was there a time when you were only studying classical music and not playing out in the clubs.
Very few times.
I’m trying to figure out about when this was. Do you know what years you were a student at either of those institutions?
USC, ’53. And the other, ’44, ’43.
Would that be before or after you recorded for the first time for Victor/Bluebird, because that’s always been unclear in all of the writing about you.
After.
Tell me about Elmer’s on North State Street.
It was a bar. Everybody came to it. We were right across from the Chicago Theatre. Right across from the State and Lake.
And were you playing by yourself, with a trio?
Playing by myself.
How did that differ from the gig at Costello’s?
It didn’t differ, just some more work.
Different clientele?
Yeah, different clientele.
How were they different?
Maybe in class. And I began to get more attention. I would get musicians from the Chicago Theatre and from the State and Lake.
There was something that I missed in my notes. In 1940, which may or may not be the case, you show up for rehearsal for Lionel Hampton’s Orchestra at the Grand Terrace. Tell me about that.

That’s true. I was working in Kankakee at the Circle Bar. Some of the musicians there, “You going to let this broad play? “ I went up there and played, so they started taking their newspapers down and listening. I played “Deep Purple” like Art Tatum. And so they said, “Heh, heh, heh, haaa..” So . . . Lionel Hampton said, “I want to hire this girl.” So Gladys [Hampton’s wife and manager] said, “You ain’t gonna hire no broad in this band.”
Was it her decision?
Yes.
How did the other men in the band feel about a woman having an opportunity to play with Hampton?

Well, they all clapped which is something unheard of. ‘Cause men don’t want to hear women play anyway. So I played that, “Heeeehhhy” and when I got through, they all clapped. And Lionel said, “We got to hire her.” Gladys said, “Uh-uhh, you ain’t gonna hire this broad in this band.”
Do you think you would have been the right pianist for that band or would you have wanted to play too much for a band of that size?
Both, I guess. . . . See who was playing, Sir Charles Thompson.
Now, I guess Illinois Jacquet was in the band at the time.
He was.
Was he supportive of you or was he fearful of you?
Supportive. When we’re in Europe, he wants me to play with him. Especially if he ain’t getting the audience. “C’mon up here girl.”
Do you think that event in 1940, was it an audition?
I just wanted to play, I already had a job.
Where were you playing?
Kankakee, a sewer in Kankakee.
To what extent were you playing outside of Chicago? Because that’s something that hasn’t been written about your life.
A lot.
How far outside Chicago were you playing?
About 40 minutes. I’d take a train and go to Kankakee.
The Circle Lounge you mentioned. Were there other clubs as well that you played in Kankakee and other cities?
No that was it at the time for Kankakee.
How was the money outside in Kankakee compared to Chicago.
It was alright. I think I got $20 more.
So, you would have been about 18 at this time.
When did you join the union?
They were separated then, weren’t they? So, when you joined the union, how much did it cost to join?
Yes. I think it cost $50.
And the dues were about how much a year?
And could you tell me, when you went outside like on the North Side, who collected the dues, the white union man or the black union man?
Let’s see, usually it would be the white.
He collected them, for his union? What did the black union have to say about that?
Yeah. He didn’t have nothing to say about that.
Did you ever play with white musicians at that time?
No.
That’s one thing that they didn’t…
They were segregated.
But I wondered who was collecting the money because I know what that means.
Tell me about your first recording session, Miss Donegan.
With Victor/Bluebird? They said that was a pretty good record, with Mayo…
Mayo Williams? He was an A&R Director for Victor.
Yeah. I did, “Piano Boogie” and “Everyday Blues.”
“Prelude in C# Minor.” How did that come about?
They wanted me to record on Decca. I recorded a lot of things for Decca but they never released them.
Was that before you recorded for Bluebird?
Around the same time.
Because I have no reference to Decca recordings in the discography. But that’s one of the limitations of discographies too. How did you meet J. Mayo Williams?
I don’t know. I guess he met me first. “I want you to record.”
How did you come into contact with Mayo Williams?
I guess he found me.
I think that’s a pretty typical story of recording artists in Chicago who recorded for Victor. So you had two 78’s that were issued, or was it just one?
Two.
And how did that change your career as a performing artist? Did that enable you to raise your fees or did it give you more visibility?
I don’t think it did anything. Just some wasted recording.
Was it a big accomplishment for you, was it something you were proud of?
I liked the technique in it. One critic says, “Ahh, more than eight to the bar.” (laughs)
Do you remember the recording process, anything about it, what the studio was like?
No, they just put the lights and say, “Go.”
How was recording these tunes different that performing them live for you?
Well, if you record it, you can rehearse when you make a mistake.
Can you tell me more about that?
Today, they say if you record something, you can erase it and re-record it.
How many takes did you usually have to do?
I don’t think I did but two or three.
I didn’t think so because you’re very articulate and you change them around each time, don’t you?
Yeah, it’s never the same.
So, did that make the engineer nervous?
It might have.
‘Cause Dorothy is Dorothy. When you first heard yourself back on the recording, did you like what you heard?
Yeah, I liked one chord in there that I played.
One chord? What was so likeable about that one chord…
I don’t know, I played the right change and it clicked.
Touch you. Can you tell me what piano they used.
I used a Baldwin.
Was it a baby grand or upright?
Baldwin. It was a baby grand. Not the nine foot.
The baby grand. What is your favorite piano while we’re here?
Steinway. I want to get a nine foot.
That’s a girl.
Miss Donegan, did you ever see your Bluebird 78 on a jukebox?
No.
Do you think it was marketed to jukebox operators?
It should have been, but it wasn’t.
Tell me about those two selections: “Piano Blues” and “Everyday Blues.”
I composed both of them. And I just started sitting at the piano and whatever came out came out. Like mixing a cake, a little bit of this and a little bit of that.
Was there any record or blues tune before that you based it on?
No.
What keys did you choose for those, do you happen to remember?
The key of C.
Is C a good key for you to play blues?
I think so. And D major too.
What is it about those keys that is well-suited to the blues?
Well, the chords fall easier.
In the recording studio, you’re limited to about three minutes that you can fit on the side of a 78. If you were playing these two tunes in a nightclub, would you play them for five or six minutes?
I might. It doesn’t matter, ‘cause you’re not recording.
Were there any other limitations of the recording studio?
No, just those two songs. They liked what they heard, so they printed it.
But they didn’t schedule you for another session. Why is that?
I don’t know. Decca did, though.
How much later?
Four or five months later. I recorded 60 tunes for them.
But they were never issued.
No, they save them ‘til I die.
Who scheduled the Decca sessions?
Milt Gabler.
Did he contact you directly or did he have someone under him do it?
I guess he did.
Let’s step back to Bluebird for a second. What was the nature of your contract with them? Was it just for one session?
Yes.
And did they have an option to do more sessions with you if they chose to?
I guess so.
Were you paid a flat fee for that session?
Yes. Mayo gave me what he wanted me to have.
What did he want you to have?
As little as possible.
Any recall on how much or how little?
Maybe $150.
And there were no royalty arrangements on that?
You never get royalties.
That’s Milt Gabler, so we’re talking the Decca sides. How about for Bluebird, through Mayo Williams.
Nothing.
Did you get paid a flat fee with him?
Yes.
About the same?
Yes.
So you recorded approximately 60 sides for Decca? Tell me about the differences in repertoire.
It’s all classical. Swinging classics.
You mentioned you and Hazel Scott popularizing this form. Was that a musical trend that was popular or is it just something that happened both in New York and Chicago?
I think she was into swinging the classics and I was in Chicago. Parallel development.
Did Hazel Scott have commercial success with recordings on swinging the classics?
I don’t think so. She was popular but not on records. Her records wouldn’t sell and mine either. That’s what my son says.
Over how long a period did you record the 60 sides with Decca?
Maybe a week.
And how many sessions might that have been?
I guess all day.

For instance, the session for Bluebird, you recorded four sides. The next listed session for commercial releases is 1946 with Continental and it looks like you did six sides. The session following that with issued commercial recordings for Continental, six sides. Would they have you do more than that in a day?
Decca did.
OK. Was there any major difference in approach in the studio on the part of the record company? Did Decca and Milt Gabler, did they do anything differently than Mayo Williams and Bluebird?
No. They just had different music.
60 sides of swinging classics, or was there blues and classical material and boogie­ woogie mixed in there as well?
Everything.

That’s a big piece that has not been written about, so that’s an important one. The last thing I wanted to cover today was what appears to be a turning point in your career in 1943 and that’s the Orchestra Hall concert. Can you tell me how that came about?

Joe Sherman wanted to put me in a concert behind Vladimir Horowitz. So I played by myself and he hit me on the behind and he said, “Go out there and lead with your left.” So I played and it was a major success.
Who else was on that bill?
Nobody.
You and Horowitz.
Well, Horowitz had played a week before. But I had outdrawn him. I can’t outdraw him now but then I did.
From what I understand, you were the first African-American musician to play Orchestra Hall.
Maybe so.
Tell me about the audience at Orchestra Hall.
I get a lot of white people. Well, white people support jazz, you know. And African- Americans don’t support it.
Was that true in 1943?
Yes.
Tell me about your performance there. What did your repertoire consist of?
Classical and boogie and, they said, . . . I drew them out the swamp. I played classical first, and then blues next and boogie last. Something for everybody.
Why do you play them in that order, or did you in 1943?
Well, you show first you didn’t learn in reform school how to play the piano. And that’s the way I do it. Play something first and, OK, now we get to the root.

You’re suggesting almost a stigma with jazz, perhaps especially with white audiences in the 1940s and perhaps continuing today. Did playing the classical music in your performances help to remove any stigma associated with jazz or stigma associated in the minds of white folks with black music?
Well, I played once for Itzal Hurok (?) and Margaret Truman was there. So, I played Rondo Capriccioso and Hurok was looking. Say, “You didn’t know she reads, did you? “ I like that, you know.
So Joe Sherman helped to arrange that gig at Orchestra Hall? At what point did he come into your professional career?
Yes. That was it after I played there ‘cause he wouldn’t give me a raise. And I stayed with him for a little while but I had to go upstairs for $750. He was only giving me $250.
Do you recall what you made for the Orchestra Hall concert?
And that was a sold out performance, wasn’t it?
Yeah, every seat was sold out.

How did you go to a sell-out crowd in Orchestra Hall from performing in Kankakee, performing with a couple dance bands and as a solo artist in the clubs? What was the process of going to that next tier and to a very major step?
Dixon Gayer of Downbeat had given me a great write-up.
Prior to the Orchestra Hall concert? Was it just on the basis of that one review?
Yes. Claudia Castor had given me a great write-up in the Chicago Tribune on the front page.
How much of it was also working with Joe Sherman and therefore, Joe Glaser’s office?
I guess they helped too. Everybody helps you.
Looking back at that performance, was that fundamentally different from what you were doing in other clubs and venues?
I guess it was a compilation of everything I had done.
Did you see it at the time as a turning point in your career?
Yes.
How about leading up to it?
Yes.
How about if it had not sold out or you didn’t get great reviews as a result of it. Do you think that you would have continued to be booked in venues of that size?
I think so. People like me anyway.
Do you think that you were at a different stage of being ready for a step up in your career? Were you just prepared at that moment?
Yes.
Was there any difference in your confidence or approach?
No.
Maturity in your style or artistic development?
No.
Time was just right?
Yes. That was it.

Today is April 6, 1998 here in Beverly Hills, California for the second day of the Smithsonian Institution Jazz Oral History Program with Dorothy Donegan conducted by Jeannie Cheatham, engineered by Matt Watson, and I’ll pass this over to Jeannie.

Dorothy, yesterday we were talking about rehearsal techniques. You know how you said you would rehearse sometimes 12 hours a day. What I’d like to know, when you would make a mistake in something you were studying, how would you take care of that?

I would hit it real hard, so I would remember where the mistake occurred. And then go back to it and work it out with two or three fingers. Every mistake has a secret to it, so you can master it. You got to keep on practicing though, ‘til you work it out. It must be worked out.
But you make the mistake again when you came to it?

Sometimes. And then I would do the mistake with three fingers rather than two. C B A D C B E D C and work it around. And then go back A G F G F E F E D… go up and down the piano ‘til I had mastered the mistake.
Did you find that also true…would you rehearse songs in different keys for that same reason?
Not necessary. I wouldn’t have to do that. I don’t have to rehearse songs to play them in different keys. Just stumble up on it.
Did you have preferred keys that you use, for instance, for the blues?
Art Tatum and I like E natural and B natural. And F sharp, which is G flat.
Would you do that only to confuse the bass player as I’ve heard? Would you change keys and play F sharp ‘cause you know bass players can’t play in F sharp?
No, I would just do it naturally.
Did you have certain keys that you prefer when you play the blues.
I like to play the blues in D natural.
Why?
I think it’s more colorful, the key. It produces better changes.
It’s a bright key.
Yes. I said, “Oooohhh, la la” C doesn’t have pretty harmonies.
That’s true. How about G?
I like to play “Rainy Day” in G.
I’ve heard you play “After Hours” and that’s also in G.
Yeah, well. That’s enough with that song. (Sings it). Yeah, G is good for that.
How did you find that Hanon, the virtuoso studies, help your playing?
It makes the fingers stronger. You can exercise the fourth and fifth fingers, which are the weakest.
Did you find Czerny the same?
Yeah, I still practice Czerny, when I’m well. And I prefer the Brahms exercises.
Which one of the masters do you prefer, like Chopin, Beethoven, Bach, Brahms…
I like Bach and Chopin. Chopin is so hard to play, oh my god, you have to play it real soft and light and fleeting.
And use the pedals, right?
Well, yeah, I could use them. But you have to keep your fingers close to the keys and finger it all the way down.
You sure know your work. When you do songs like “Tenderly” which is almost a kind of a song you can use pianistically, can take it in and out of what I call a classical type
sound. What would you do if you had a chance to play “Tenderly”? I’ve heard you go in and out of different…
I start in E natural and get all the meat out of it. Then I may go back to D and then I may go back to G.
You know, talking all these keys, which is really rough on most bass players, I’m telling you.
Well, you got to get a bass player first.
Who was your favorite bass player that you had the least problem with that could really…
I liked John Clayton.
Tell us about John Clayton.
He was very good. He wasn’t the funkiest, but he was accurate. And then Ray Brown. I haven’t played much with him. Jon Burr, my bass player, was pretty good.
Where was he from?
Upstate New York. He wasn’t funky enough for me.
Do you find that from different parts of the country that you get a bass player that plays certain ways?
I guess so, yeah. “Put a little more Christian McBride in it.”
You like that little boy, huh?
Yeah.
How about George Duvivier?
He was good in his time.
Did you ever play with Jo Jones, old man Jo Jones?
Oh yeah, he threw a stick at me once.
Why did he throw a stick at you?

I picked the time up. And he says, “Johnson’s on the whozits,” so he threw a stick at me and it landed in the piano instead of my head. He was aiming for my head. So I took the stick, I got up and said, “How dare you throw a stick in my piano?” So I took the stick and hit him in the head, it landed perfectly, you know. And he kept on playing. People thought it was part of the show.
Yes. He really loved you, you know.
I did, too. That’s one funeral I made. I said, “Jo Jones couldn’t pack a club but he could pack his funeral.”
That’s true.
Every drummer was there. Were you there?
He told us not to come to his funeral.
Oh, it was raining and slushy. But I made it. I changed trains and everything to get there.
What other drummers were there?
It would be safe to say who wasn’t there.
Max Roach?
Oh yes.
Grady Tate?
Grady Tate. They were all there.
Have you ever played in an all-girl band, trio or…
Maybe with the Sweethearts of Rhythm, but that didn’t last long.
How long?
About a week. I think it was over before then.
Is it because you don’t prefer playing with…
Women? Well, why have sexist musicians? They’re either musicians or they’re not.
I agree.
They say all girls groups or all women’s groups. Just put them with the men, they’re all musicians.
You’re a girl after my own heart. When you stopped studying your classical music, did you miss the studies?
I never stopped. When I would play the jazz to make some money, you know you have to eat. It’s necessary that you eat, I’d keep on studying and studying and studying.
Yes. Can I ask you, do you think that if you had gone to Paris when you were a young person that you would have fared better in your career in the United States?
I don’t know. ‘Cause they only had one Josephine Baker. I guess Paris thought that was enough.
Have you ever played there, Paris?
Oh sure. I played the Meridien Hotel, La Petit Journal. They liked me in Paris, but they make you play…
You played in Paris and you were treated well…
Yes, but they want you to play with French musicians. I didn’t like that. I started crying.
Why, what difference did you find?
Well, they can’t even play jazz. They don’t play jazz.
Rhythmically, is that what they’re lacking?
Rhythmically, any kind of way.
Even harmonically?

Yeah, see what they do is they play with Americans and they get a name and the next week, they got the trio. They had the Hot Club of France, I guess they were notable exceptions. Still would rather the brothers, you know. American, playing with them. They gonna play jazz, you know.
Did you play with Jimmy Woode?
Oh, did I. He was drunk on me sometimes, but I loved him.
I did too.
Yeah, even drunk. I’d say, I’d fire him, but I’d say, “Come back tomorrow.” He used to play, “Sometimes I Feel Like a Motherless Child,” and he’d be crying.
I think he was homesick.
If you’re travelling in Europe you still have to find home in America, you’re still an American. And black, don’t forget that.
I won’t forget it, I remember. Tell me, what were some of your favorite foods in France?

I guess I liked to eat in the best restaurants. And I liked to eat in Switzerland because they put gravy on everything. And what’s this musician out of Chicago, he’d throw the food up in the air, say “Everything about this food stinks!”
Who was that?
What’s that crazy drummer’s name in Chicago? He’s about 85.
He live there?
No, he come over there and play.

And then they tell us, none of the American blacks can eat in a restaurant because of what he did. I said, “Well I’m gonna eat in here or else go home.” And they said, “Well you can eat in here but the rest can’t. “ I said, “If that’s the problem, I’ll still go home.”
Getting back to your different techniques, when you were playing did you prefer a certain type of piano? A certain brand did you ask for?
I didn’t know the difference back then. I took what I could get. People would give you a piano to play on, I’d say, “This ain’t no good.” They’d say, “They tuned it, so it must be alright.”
They didn’t care about the touch of the piano, the quality?
They were lucky to have a piano.
I’d like to go back to where we left off yesterday and that was around the Orchestra Hall concert in 1942. Was that one of the high points of your musical career?

I think so. Here was a girl from the South Side with red hair, playing on the stage by herself in front of 2000 people. And to outsell Vladimir Horowitz, I thought that was something. And this promoter, Joe Sherman, wanted me to stay a slave for life. But I said, “I’ll stay with you for a certain while but if I get a raise, I got to go.”
How long did you stay with him?
About a month or so. I gave him a chance to recoup his investment. Then I said, “I got to go.”
Now, Time Magazine did a great big write-up on that concert at Orchestra Hall and I guess, gave you some national exposure, is that true?
Yes.
How did that change things for you?
Well, I started being offered more money, which is always nice.
How much more money were you making?
Well, I went from $250 to $750.
And that’s per week?
Oh yeah.
Now, yesterday you mentioned playing Kankakee, Illinois. Did your bookings extend further beyond Chicago and Kankakee after the national exposure.
This was before the national exposure.
When did you start to really get booked outside of Chicago?
After I made a picture with Cab Calloway.
What other opportunities did the Orchestra Hall concert present to you?
You get national exposure in the newspaper and I guess you’d get the movies.
It seems that about this time that Art Tatum became aware of your presence and your talent. Can you discuss how you came to meet him?
Well, that lady right there, her husband brought him up to my house.
That lady being…
Lois Gayle. And her husband was Rozelle. So they brought Tatum up to my house on St. Lawrence.
Tell me about that experience. They just gave you a call and said we’re bringing Tatum over?
Yeah, Rozelle said Tatum was coming up. And so, he came up to see me. He said, “That woman, you never know what she is going to do.” (Laughs).
Were you intimidated by him?
I was flattered that he came up, you know. How he could do it so easy. I could do what he did but it would be a little harder.
Do you think he was scoping out the competition that might come his way?
Oh yes. He respected me, and so did the fellows in the block. See, we all lived on St. Lawrence and we’d have those cutting sessions.
Tell me about that.
Well, everybody played what they knew and if you won, you’d cut everybody.
Where would they be held?
Basements and dumps and houses.
How long would they last? What time would they start?
About 10, 11:00 and last all night.
[Track 6]
So, Tatum began to mentor you and show you the ropes.
Yeah and I’d be under him like white on rice, trying to learn all the nuances and the half steps, the whole steps and how he would finger. And had this one (thumb) going underneath.
Tell me about that. Describe that in detail.
Oh, I don’t want to divulge my secret. That’s one of the tricks he had. He’d have three up here and one underneath here, fingering all the way down.
And what would that allow him to do?
Go fast. He could play so beautifully.
Have you ever seen anyone else since or before use their thumb in that way?
No, there hasn’t been anybody else. There never will be anybody else. He was first, second and third in my book.
What other tricks did he have in his style?
