Gee, I’m gonna tell you my style pretty soon. I guess he knew how to move the thumb. The thumb would go underneath the other fingers starting from the left. And he says, “If it don’t fit, don’t force it.” The softer you play the faster you could play, is that right?
What other fingerings did he show you that made you modify your approach to the instrument?
He would show me how to stride. That wasn’t his main thing though, stride. And to keep this finger stiff so you can catch the G and the C going down.
That’s the pinky finger.
Yeah, it’s ready when you want it.
Did he correct you on anything you were doing wrong or did he just show you how to develop more quickly?
He showed me how to do it more quickly and not to hit the piano so hard. You hit it easily and softer.
Did you feel that he wanted to show you everything he knew, or was he holding back some tricks that he wasn’t going to show anybody?
He held back a lot of stuff. I loved the way he carried his money. He carried it in five different pockets. The 5’s, the 10’s, the 50’s and the 100’s. He knew where everything was.
Was that a result of his vision problems?
Yes, he had a good memory, too. He could play pinochle. He was a genius.
Were there any things beyond his playing that he taught you, taught you about the business or about booking or promoting yourself?
No, he never discussed his bookings. He was just good to be around. I always found him very informative, you know. And I was glad to be around him.
Specifically, what did he show you that you incorporated into your playing?
All the other things that I told you about.
How long did you really work with Art Tatum?
I worked with him in Chicago and worked with him in New York. I used to go up to Minton’s and we’d have cutting contests up there. And eat chicken and waffles and sausage.
Was Tatum a competitive player or was he so far beyond everyone else that he had nothing to worry about?
He had nothing to worry about. As a matter of fact, he didn’t have to compete, he’d just play. One musician said, “God is in the house.” He could cut us with one hand.
Tatum is reported as saying, “Dorothy is the only woman who can make me practice.”
That’s true.
Did he say that to you?
Yeah. And made Hazel Scott leave the country.
Now, his comment, “Dorothy is the only woman who can make me practice,” was that a compliment or is that a little bit of a back-handed insult?
Well, I guess it’s both but I like the compliment.
Do you believe that he would say that there’s any man that could make him practice?
He didn’t think about them too much. He wasn’t worried. There was Billy Taylor and who else during that time? And Oscar [Peterson].
Do you think that there’s anything that you might have shown Tatum that he might have lifted and worked into his playing?
Possibly. Well, see, I never play a piece the same way. So maybe some of my pieces he may have caught things that I didn’t know he was listening for.
According to my notes, this would have been 1943, around the age of 21 for you. Is that about right?
Yes.
Now, one of the results of the exposure from the Orchestra Hall concert, led to an offer of a five-year movie contract with MGM. Tell me about that.

And that greedy agent, his name was Corkscrew Gervish, I called him. He took the deal from United Artists, $3000 a week and I only did a week. With MGM, I had $750 a week for seven years and he didn’t take it.
And this was to appear in movies similar to the United Artists release?
I would take anything.
Was this kind of revue-type music movies?
Yeah. Where you can be inserted in a picture and deleted too.
Tell me about what you mean by being deleted.
Like if you’re in a movie, like if you play a Lena Horne and that, you can delete it for the South or for Southern audiences and the plot would not be disturbed.
So the MGM offer was before or after the United Artists?
I think it was during the same time.
When did you go out to Hollywood?
What part of the year?
I guess in the middle of the year. Me and my mother went to do “Sensations of ‘45” with Cab Calloway, Eleanor Powell, Woody Herman, and Dennis O’Keefe.
How about Sophie Tucker and W.C. Fields, were they in there?
Yes, and I was in a circus.
Tell me about that.

I was playing opposite Gene Rodgers, who was a great pianist. And Cab had his self between us both, “C’mon Dorothy, C’mon Gene.” And he was shaking his hair. That’s what he contributed. We were doing the playing and he was shaking his hair.
Do you think you portrayed yourself well on film? Did your talent as a recording artist and as a stage artist transfer well to the screen?
I think so. They could see my feet stomping and I’m doing all this, you know striding. So I did pretty good.
Did you have to wear anything different that you would in your normal stage appearance?
No, I wore a gown. I think it was one of Pola Negri’s gowns. And I had my hair in an upsweep and a gardenia on the right-hand side.
Was it simply a musical part or did you have spoken lines?
No lines. It was just a sequence that could be always deleted.
So, did that open up new doors for you?

It opened up a door for me in New York, I played Loyce State (?) with the picture and they said that if I didn’t appear with the picture I would never do another film again. So I appeared with the picture.
Now, appearing with the picture, that’s not something that happens anymore. Can you tell me what that would…you would appear at the screening of the movie?
Well, if they showed a picture, then I’d come on with a stage show.
With other performers from the film, Cab Calloway and such…
Cab didn’t appear. Some comics, off-beat comics you know.
What happened after “Sensations of ‘45”—were there other attempts at film?
No.
In fact, I’ve read in other accounts that there was another film made but I’ve never seen its title or anything. Can you clarify that? Did you ever do another movie?
No.
Where did you go from there? What happened next?
I guess I went back to Chicago.

Somewhere around this time, it’s never dated, you were doing some package tours with both the International Sweethearts of Rhythm and Jackie “Moms” Mabley. Was that the same tour, were they on the package together with you?
I must have done two theatres with them. Jackie “Moms” Mabley, she said, she’d stop the show and say, “Follow that.”
Tell me more about her.

She’d put her teeth in the glass, perform, she was a comedian, you know. She’d perform and stop the show. So, that’s how you learn how to stop a show, with performers like that. And then there was another performer, Peg Leg Bates, had one leg. He’d say, “Let me break this other leg for you.”
On that kind of package, what would the order be, the order of artists?
They would close it. ‘Cause I don’t think I could close it then. Now I could.
At what point in your career where you able to close it?
When I appeared against Teddy Wilson and Thelma Carpenter.
When was that?

’54.’55. George Gewee (?) said I called and asked for the job, you know. So, he gave me $500, I said, “Oh, I’ll make this due.” He said, “Oh, you gotta pay your men out of it.” I said, “That’s alright too.” So, I played against Thelma Carpenter and Teddy Wilson. And Thelma
Carpenter took all the time. I said, “You can take all night, it ain’t gonna make no difference.” So I got on there and stopped that show cold.
What happened after you stole the show?
She never spoke to me again. She said, “Dorothy stole the show but I closed it.” I said, “Closed it?” Yeah.
How about the International Sweethearts of Rhythm, where were those two shows that you performed?
At the Regal and the Fox Theatre.
The Fox Theatre being where?
Detroit. No, it was the Paradise. They call that the Chittlin’ Circuit, TOBA. Tough On Black Actors.

Now, on the chittlin’ circuit, it would frequently also visit The Apollo, The Howard Theatre in DC, the Royal Theatre in Baltimore. Why did this bill with the Sweethearts and Moms Mabley not travel to New York, Baltimore, Pittsburgh?
I don’t think nobody asked for them, you know. You got to be asked for, you know.
Differences in the audience between Detroit and Chicago?
Yes.
Tell me about that.

Detroit was tough. The Howard Theatre was tougher: “Don’t be playin’ any of that classical music here.” And that Royal in Baltimore—the Ink Spots played there once and there was a big rat that ran across the stage. So somebody took out a gun and shot it. They thought it was a cat, you know. And Bill Kenny said, “Whoaaaaaaaa” and they ran off the stage.
What were some of your favorite clubs to play at this point, somewhere in the mid­ 40’s? What were your preferences? If you could pick a venue to play in the 1940’s, what were your favorites?
Any place that paid a lot of money, that’s a favorite.
Can you tell me about the wartime entertainment tax against entertainers? 20% tax on entertainers during the war years.

I don’t remember that. Unless it was on me. They claimed that I wiggled when I played and there should be a tax on it, you know. So the union says, “Well, she can wiggle as long as she keeps playing the piano.” Some of the women pianists were kind of jealous.
Did that get you off the hook and keep you categorized as a musician?
Oh yeah. And one of the owners said, “My wife don’t want to come in here since she’s here.” I said, “I know she don’t mind spending the money I made.”
Tell me about the wiggling, the hip shaking, the arm flourishes.

I’d be playing and I’d be wiggling and most people wanted to sit in the back rather than in the front. So people like the Duke and Duchess of Windsor would come in, Tallulah Bankhead, Ronald Reagan and his wife, Robert Montgomery and his wife, they all want to see me.
When did some of those aspects become a part of your performance style?
I guess during then. Of course I don’t do it as much now, I don’t have the energy. And I find, the more piano playing you do, you don’t have to do that.
Were you ever criticized for that?
Yes, some people criticized it, you know. So I said, “Well, as long as I play the piano, I can shake. Some people don’t have nothing to shake.”
Who would criticize you for that?
The other women pianists.
Why is that? Did they not have something to shake?
No, their behind was kind of flat.
Most musicians have superstitions. Do you have any superstitions?
You can’t put your hat on my bed.
Can’t put your hat on your bed. Why?
That means the show’s gonna close.
Is that so?
And you can’t whistle in my dressing room.
Why is that?
It’s bad luck.
Can you tell me something—was it an advantage for you to be light-skinned versus a darker-skinned entertainer?
In Europe, a darker skinned woman has a better opportunity than a light one.
Why do you think that is?
They want to help our own. They want a colored woman. They say they got the light woman at home.
How about in the U.S.?
In the United States, they want the entertainers to be dark, especially on TV.
Really. And during your time when you did movies, when you were young, like just starting out in Chicago and all, did you find most showgirls that danced and all were a particular shade?
In the Cotton Club, all them women were real light. Like a woman my color or yours, we couldn’t get work there. They had to be “high yella,” an “oreo.”
I understand. Did you have a lot of stage door men standing around waiting to take you out while you were playing?
Yeah, those who weren’t working were around there. If they were working, they didn’t come around. Show women get nothing but pimps usually.
No rich white persons or persons of color with limousines that wanted to wine and dine you?
Not really. They get people that have good manners, they pull the chairs back, ‘cause they don’t have a job so they have time to learn their manners.

Miss Donegan, according to my notes, somewhere about 1945 or 1946, obviously following “Sensations of ‘45” you were performing solo in Los Angeles and, this may have been at the Latin Quarter? Is that correct?
I think that was before then.
A revue program with chorus girls and dancers, the De Marcos as dancers?
Yes, and Benny Fields and Blossom singing. I was in a show called “Star Time.”
I think this is what leads to “Star Time”—comedians Jerry Lester, Lou Holtz. Tell me about Lou Holtz and how he came into your career.

He showed me how to walk out on a stage, Lou Holtz did. And I think he owned a piece of the San Francisco Hotel. But he showed me how to walk out. And he said, “If you give love in your eyes, then you’ll get love in response back.” And I was in the show with him, the Berry brothers got sick so I took their place. They were working too hard, like Buddy Collette, you know.
So, Lou Holtz took you back to New York to appear in “Star Time”?
Yes, and the De Marcos, and Benny Fields, and one of those Blossoms, Blossom Seals. So I learned about show business from them, the vaudeville stuff. ‘Cause they knew all that.
Tell me about “Star Time.”
It was a play, it didn’t run too long. I don’t think it had a book, a story.
How was it different from just a revue?
It was just a revue. And I was the only black performer in it.
Where did it run?
New York, and then it ran in Philadelphia. But it was soon to close.
Do you happen to remember which theatres in New York and Philadelphia?
No.
What would you perform in your section of that performance?
I’d do something like the “Prelude in C# Minor” or else “Minute Waltz.” You’d swing that and do a boogie-woogie.

Did you feel you were being locked into a certain style in your performances in the movie, “Sensations of 1945” and then “Star Time”? Were you expected in all of your performances to play the classics, to swing the classics and then to play jazz or did you have more freedom in your performances?
Well, I picked the numbers but I picked the numbers that would sell. They liked classical and they liked jazz, so you can’t miss with the combination. You got to get somebody.
How long did that run for?
About six to eight weeks.

Miss Donegan, about this time, 1946 or 47, according to the discographies, you were recording in New York for Continental. The session is undated, solo piano “Some of These Days,” “Kilroy Was Here,” “Schubert’s Boogie-Woogie,” “How High the Moon,” “The Man I Love,” “Two Loves Was One Too Many For Me.” Any recollection of these dates?
I don’t remember that one. “Two Loves Was One Too Many For Me.”
Any recollection of that?
I’d have to learn that again.
Any differences in recording for Continental than back for Bluebird?
I think I liked that number “Yesterday” that I played for Continental. My brother said he liked it.

That was another Continental session from 1946, September. That was, according to the discography here, a trio…well, you did some solos and some trio work on that earlier session, September 1946…with Carl “Flat Top” Wilson on bass and Oliver Coleman on drums. Can you tell me anything about that? How were they?
Fair.
Anything else?
That’s it.

Tell me about, after “Star Time,” 1946 or 47, maybe you can tell me, you had another opportunity for a stage performance. A leading role in a Broadway-bound musical. It had a run in Connecticut in the summer theatre there.
That’s “Star Time.”
That’s “Star Time” as well? According to the notes I’ve got, the production did not do well, never made it to Broadway.
No, it was with Jane White, Walter White’s daughter. She was trying to boss everybody in the show. It didn’t have it, to go the extra 10 years.
Do you recall how much you got paid?
About $750.
$750 a week? How many performances a week?
About eight.
So, matinees on the weekend?
Yeah. I like to work short. Work smarter, not harder.
On the “Star Time” production, were you required to stay around for the entire performance? Or could you come in, do your performance and take off?
I could go home.
How long was your segment in the “Star Time” production?
Around eight or nine weeks I think.
No, I mean in a given night?
I could do as long as I wanted.

What can you tell me about…at this time, 1946, ‘47 after the war…the possibility to cross over from being a musical artist, a recording artist to a film artist to someone hopefully on their way to Broadway. Was it easier then than it is now?
I think it was. Whatever the job called for, you know that’s what you did.
Were you anxious to cross over into other venues than being just a recording artist?
You were anxious to just get work. You weren’t thinking about other venues, you were just thinking about getting work. You’re supposed to get work.
Who were the most successful performers who started as musicians and made it on either Broadway or musical stage or movies at this time in the ‘40’s.
Oscar hadn’t started then, had he? . . . Nat Cole.
Do you think Nat Cole opened doors for other African-American performers as he crossed over into television, film…
I don’t think so because in show business, they only made one of us at a time. And when they mess up, they’d book another one.
When you say that, how long would the average career of that one artist at a time be in vogue before they fell from popularity and the industry was looking for another one?
I think as long as the public liked them. You could be Jay Gould one day and Jay Bird the next in the same day.
One piece of information that I’ve come across in some of the writings about that I’m very unclear about says that you studied Psychology at the University of Chicago in the 1940’s, yes or no?
Yes.
Tell me about that.
I had a boyfriend that was going there so me and him would study together. And I’d help him with some of his problems.
Were you enrolled there?
Yes.
How did studying Psychology at the University of Chicago differ from studying Sociology at USC?
It’s all the same. Every story got three different sections. And instruction is still instruction.
Did you have any professional goals in the field of psychology?
Not particularly. I just wanted to be knowledgeable. When people say “Van Gogh” or “The Rorschach Test,” I wanted to know what they were talking about.
How long did you study at the University of Chicago?
Not too long.
1948 you married your first husband. You didn’t mention by name yesterday, would you do that?
John T. McClain, Sr.
And that marriage lasted how long?
About 15 years. Too long.
Were there any good times with him that you want to document?
No, it looked like I did all the work. And he just went on the road with me.
To what extent did he try to navigate your business decisions? Did he serve as your manager at any time?
No, he wanted me to play in his club free.
You talked about that yesterday. Were there any other attempts for you to get movie work or stage work?
No.
Didn’t you pursue more films or stage work?
Sometimes I would get tired of playing and didn’t want to work much.
And what would you do during those times? How would you continue to pay the bills?
I would go shopping and practice. I like to go shopping.
Tell me about that. That seems to be one of your hobbies.
They say, “Shop ‘til you drop.” But I understand when you go shopping you won’t have much money. But I love to shop. Still do. I don’t do it too much now.
“Shop ‘til you drop.” Tell me something—did you have a preference for long gowns when you played or short gowns or whatever was in style?
Some periods I’d go through long ones and then the next one I’d go through shorter.

Even though sometimes you were on very high stages and women sometimes have to make a choice because of the workplace, as far as the stages are concerned, and make adjustments. Did you have to go through all that?
No.
How about shoes—high heels?
I’d have to get good shoes, ‘cause I’d break the heels.
Can you tell me some of your favorite designers?
Chanel, St. John, Versace.
You’re really hip.
I was in Paris and picked out a blouse. The woman says, “That’s silk.” I said, “Well, put it on me.”
She put it on you?
Yeah.
Did you ever learn to drive?

Yeah, but I drove so bad ‘til on the highway, the police would say, “Pull over, lady,” on the loudspeaker. So I must have been driving 15 miles an hour. Finally, I met the officer, “Lady, why do you drive so bad?” So, he says, “You’re the worst driver I’ve ever seen.” I said, “What color?” “Any! Any!” I said, “Well, mister, if you let me get away with this I won’t drive no more . . . How much time I got?”

You know what I’d like to know? You were very fortunate because most women, especially if they’re alone on the road, have to either have very good friends that drive or that drive themselves. You seem to ride around in a lot of limousines.
Well, see I would always take a plane.
And when you go back and forth from the hotel to the job.
A cab.
Did you have a set cab driver for, like, if you had to stay somewhere six or seven weeks, did you have one guy that would pick you up all the time or you’d just go out …
No.
Just go out and hail one?
Just get a cab.
In New York?
(Give) the doorman a dollar and he’ll get you a cab.
So, where would you stay in comparison to where you would play?
When I played at Tavern on the Green, I stayed at the Marriott. Real good hotels.
Yes. How about the early days, your early days in New York?
I stayed at the best.

Stayed at the best. Yes. That’s why you’re my idol. Did you have a chance to eat in the places where you worked or would they have a special table for you or would they try to tell you to go back in the kitchen and all that?
No, no kitchen.
No kitchen for Dorothy?
No. I’d just eat where the guests were. Of course, I didn’t mind eating with the fellas sometimes. But they gave them bad food for a reasonable price.
What are the comparisons between the food out front and the food in the back?
The food out front is prepared differently. The musicians get food that’s like you got rid of the things in the ice box. They had specials.
And they gave musicians the specials?
Yes.
I’d like to know what you think was the crowning point in your career? What was the most thrill for you as far as reaching a certain peak in your career?
Being invited to play before the President of the United States.
You’ll have to tell us about that.

Thelonious Monk had heard me in Switzerland. So, he asked me would I like to play at the White House. I said “Sure.” He said, “Well, I’ll let you know when I get back to America.” So, when I got back to America, he say, “It’s official.” But I noticed in the paper, they didn’t announce me. So, I learned later on the reason why. They say, the rest of them wouldn’t show up. So, I kept it under my hat . . .
Which President was this?
Clinton. I played the Newport Jazz Festival.
Did you have a special dress you bought?
I had dresses.
What did you pick out to wear?
I had a silver coat and a Chanel copy baseball hat.
A silver raincoat and what kind of a hat?
A Chanel copy baseball hat.
What kind of shoes?
Rhinestone shoes.
Silver rhinestones?
And a bugle beaded jet top and a black sequined skirt.
Oh my. When you arrived in Washington DC, did they have a car waiting for you?
Yeah, the Secret Service met us and took us to the Capitol Hotel. And old Herbie Hancock was there, Wynton Marsalis, and Joshua Redman and Red Mitchell. Everybody.
They were all there. So, they picked you up in the hotel and took you to the White House. Did they make you have credentials or something you had to show?
You had to go through a screening.
What kind of screening?
Oh, they took your fingerprints and everything.
Oh they did? Then, would they take you into the dining room or did they make you wait in the anteroom?
I guess anteroom.
Until your turn?
Yes.
So, who came on first?
I don’t know.
When did you play?
I followed Rosemary Clooney. And then Herbie Hancock had to follow me.
He had to follow you?
He was disgusted. His lip dropped down to his thing.
What did you choose to play for the President?
They only gave me 10 minutes, so I played everything I knew in 10 minutes.
Did the President look pleased?
Yeah, I got a standing ovation.
Marvelous.
And Bobby McFerrin, they were all frowning.
Why were they frowning?
I got that standing ovation, they couldn’t top that. USA Today says, “You stole the show, thanks, you stole the show.” And they all stood up. I was all by myself.
What did you do, take a bow?
Yes, I bowed to the President, then I bowed to Hillary.
Wonderful. So, you think that was about the high point of your career?
I think so. It sounds like a closer.
You could still have a movie, you know, of your life.
When you gonna do that?
Miss Donegan, can you tell me why the celebration at the White House was so important to you? Why was that the high point?
Well people all over the country saw it. They call you up. They don’t call you ‘til they see you on TV.
How about the presence of your musical colleagues, there, was that important to you?
Not really, ‘cause they don’t want me on the bill anyway and I know it. So, I had to get on the bill and get my money and get out. ‘Cause Herbie Hancock wants to run everything.
(laughs)
Were there any other events or awards or things that you’ve been honored with that…
I got a doctorate from the University of Maryland.
Tell me about that.

The President of the school heard me do a performance so he said, “I like you.” So, he wanted me to teach at the school, he said he had run out of money. So I said, “There are other ways to pay me.” So, they gave me a doctorate from the University of Maryland at Eastern Shore.
I understand that you have been a student at the University of Maryland for master classes?
Yeah, well, I go to the one at College Park and they have piano classes every year. I get to dress nice and learn to…
So, you’re always a student there but never an instructor.
You can always learn something.
What do you learn from those master classes?
When somebody else does something, you learn the way they do it. And you add what you find from them to what you know.
Would you compare any of the learning to your relationship to Art Tatum.
It’s a different structure.
How is it different?
We play classical music, no jazz there. But I learned a lot from them.

I’ve got some questions here about more sessions from the middle part of your career. Or some of the clubs you played. There’s a card from 1951, a publicity card that was used, put out by the Music Corporation of America…
They used to handle me.
Who was handling you there?
Larry Funk. And you got the same salary whether you played there or not. Every job was the same salary.
And how much was it at the time?
$1300 a week.
Was that good money compared to some of the previous gigs you’d had?
It was a good idea if you want security but I wanted more money.

Some of the prestigious venues that were listed on that card: In New York, Café Society; Hollywood, the Trocadero; Chicago, The Latin Quarter and Oriental Theatre; St. Louis, the Chase Hotel; in Detroit, the Downtown Theatre; Los Angeles, Orpheum Theatre. It also mentions the film, “Sensations of 1945.” Some pretty good venues there.
Yeah.
Any preferences for those?
Not really.
All the same.
All the same. It’s still work.
In the late 1950’s, were you shuttling back and forth between Los Angeles and New York? Would you split your time between the two cities?
I played the Embers in New York.
And I understand that you had a 10-year contract with them.
Yes.
How did that come about?
Well, they didn’t want to hire me but they hired me. People like people who do business. If you don’t do any business, it’s no good. So that’s how I got the contract.
Ralph Watkins was the owner?
Yes.
Did he do the booking?
Yeah, and Mo Louis (?).
Who were some of the other artists who would be playing at The Embers?
Jonah Jones, Hazel Scott, Joe Bushkin, Jo Jones, Teddy Wilson.
You played there 16 weeks a year. How many weeks at a time would you play in a
Four weeks at a time.
So, four months of your year would be at The Embers in New York. Where were you living when you played there?
I stayed in a hotel. Maybe the Park Sheridan.
Some of the other venues, the London House in Chicago?
That was a good one. They had blueberry muffins there. He didn’t want to play on the bill with me.
Who was this?
George Shearing. They wanted to put me on the bill, he said, “Uh-uhhh, I don’t know her.” They put in Barbara Carroll or someone like that.
The Round Table in New York.
I played there with Mel Torme.
Was Mel performing with you on the same bill?
On the same bill.
Would you open or would you close?
I think I’d open.
Were there differences between the audience at The Round Table and The Embers?
I think so.
Different kind of crowd? How so?
The audiences at The Round Table were more sophisticated. They’re cabaret-ers.
In playing to that audience, what would you play differently than you would play at The Embers?
Nothing really.
Can you tell me a little bit about how you read an audience and give them what they want, especially considering different kinds of venues, different cities?
Oh, that’s my secret.
Give us a hint.
Well, you hit one or two notes and hear the reaction. Or sometimes you have to ask them what they like to hear. But you usually know what the audience likes after you play one or two numbers.
One thing I’m unsure of from the liner notes and articles—I believe, did Jo Jones or J.C. Heard ever play in your trio’s?
Yeah, J.C. Heard used to be a boyfriend of mine.
When was this? J.C. Heard? Tell me about him.

They called him “Swee-dee-dee.” And he was sort of on the pimpy side. But that didn’t hurt me, you know. But he was a good drummer. So, we’d be on the road. I discovered you don’t go with people you work with. You can’t ‘S’ where you eat. And so pretty soon, that broke up.
How long did it take before you learned that?
About six or eight months, a year.
Did you continue to work with him or did you just break off the relationship?
No, he went his own separate way. See, he wanted to be a leader and I wanted to be a leader, so it’s not going to work. There’s only one leader.
So you only played with him for about eight months. How about Jo Jones?
Jo Jones was sort of a mentor. He was psychic, that’s what Jimmy says. He liked to talk rough to you. “Dancers on the whoozits, whoozits on the whatsits.” He threw a stick at me, you got that?
We got that.
But he was a great person. I went to his funeral. It took me two days to get there.

I wanted to ask you about live recordings. You recorded live sides for Capitol in 1958, ‘59 I believe. In the 1960’s, you started recording for Roulette. 1960, you made a recording at The Round Table with Larry Rice on drums and Doc Jones on bass. Later on, 1962, you recorded live at The Embers on Roulette. Can you tell me the difference having your records recorded live and recording in the studio. What was your preference, how are they different?

When you record, I think it’s better in the studio because you don’t hear the tinkling of the glasses and people chatting. When you record live, you hear everything. What they ate for breakfast and what they didn’t.

Now many of your recordings have been in live settings, probably because you’re such a wonderful live performer. Are there elements of your stage persona or performance style that don’t come across in a studio recording?
Well, that doesn’t come across at all, it’s just playing comes across, ‘cause you can’t see me wiggle.
You also don’t hear the crowd respond.
No. What you hear is what you get.
Do you think that the studio recordings, where what you hear is what you get, reflect your talent?
Sometimes.
Have there been any particular recordings that you’re especially proud of, that you feel really capture all of who you are as an artist?
My brother said “Yesterday” captured some of it. Many of them do and some don’t. Sometimes I say, “Oh I should have had more feeling.” ‘Course, you’re not right every day.

I’d like to go through the discography on certain dates where the rhythm section is unknown, just to see if you have any recollection to fill in some blanks historically. First one, “Jazz, Live and Boogie.” Unknown location and date, recorded for Pontiac. “Schubert’s Boogie- Woogie,” “Tin Pan Alley Boogie.” This is listed after a 1946 or ‘47 date and before a 1953 date. Any recollection of that?
No.

Here’s one, seven sides recorded for Jubilee, about the same time, somewhere in the late ‘40’s, early ‘50’s. It says “No details.” “Up a Lazy River,” “I Can’t Give You Anything But Love,” “Dancing on the Ceiling,” “Happiness is a Thing Called Joe,” “September Song,” “St. Louis Blues” “I Get a Kick Out of You.” Any recollection of where that might have been?
Let’s see, that would have been with Jo Jones. I don’t remember.

There were a number of recordings that were reissued by Rosetta Wrights (?) on Rosetta Records, on a cassette I believe called “Dorothy Romps,” piano retrospective, 1953­ 1979, something like that. None of them seem to have any information. “Dorothy Rocks,” “Minuet in G,” “Donegan Walk,” “Just in Time.”
Well, she snatched recordings from the rest of the records and then put them out on her label.
Did she pay royalties on those?
She didn’t give me royalties, she just paid me a flat sum.
So she paid you.
Yeah.
How much, if you don’t mind me asking?
Not enough.
Could you tell me why so few recordings of your music are commercially available at this point?
Well, my son, who is a great record producer—he produced Janet Jackson and Dr. Dre and people like that…
Who was this and what did he say?
It’s the rich one. John Jr. John McClain, Jr. He records artists for A&M and Polygram.
And what did he tell you about…
It’s an economy of notes.
Meaning what?
It isn’t how much you play, it’s how little you play.
Do you know how many records you have out on the market these days?
No, I’m not aware.

I was trying to find a few and came up with a few recent ones from the recordings on the SS Norway on Chiaroscuro Records, 1990, ‘91 and ‘92 performances. There’s also that recording that we just mentioned, on Rosetta Records, the cassette. There is also one that was recorded in 1980 called “The Explosive Dorothy Donegan.”
Yeah, Gus Gutierrez (?)
Tell me about these recordings, do they reflect your talent?
So-so.
What changes would you make in your recorded output?
I’d plan it more. See, you can’t go and play like it’s a jam session. I think that’s one of the faults. It has to be planned.
Did you even do a session where you had that time to plan ahead and figure out what you were going to do?
I don’t think so. If you caught me right, you caught me right. If you caught me wrong, it wasn’t.
For listeners who are going to listen to your records into the next century—25 years from now, 50 years from now—what are they going to take from those recordings of you that are available?
I think they’d like them really. People who do buy them, you know I always say it’s music that has snob appeal and I appeal to that kind of audience.
Explain that to me.
Snob appeal.
Why do you recordings have that snob appeal?
They combine the classical influences and the jazz. So, that’s how my music would sound.
In the 1960’s, many of the supper clubs that you had been playing in began to close. How did that affect your career?
Well, I would cry but everything doesn’t last forever. Life doesn’t last forever. So you have to wait ‘til the time comes back.

Supper clubs are something that as a rule, don’t exist today like they did. Are there any other places that opened up as a result—are there any other sectors of the entertainment economy, or venues, that started booking the kinds of acts that the supper clubs used to?
The Copley Plaza, places like that. And the Village Vangate [Village Gate], the Village Vanguard. Some of the clubs on the West Side, Mikell’s Pub, Jimmy Weston’s.
When did you start playing some of those others, Jimmy Weston’s for example?
I guess ’56, ’57.
Did you ever have opportunities open up in Europe as things dried up in the States, especially in the ‘60’s?
I don’t think so. Usually people call you in Europe when they need you. I guess that’s every club owner. I get more gigs now than…
I read somewhere that you got in trouble with some of the European bookers for demanding and commanding the salaries that the male musicians were getting paid.
I didn’t get in trouble, I just said I should make the same money if I’m playing better or as well. And staying in better hotels.
Did you get that?
Yeah, ‘cause I wasn’t gonna stay in the dumps. They put the musicians in dumps you know.
How did the male musicians feel about you commanding the same salaries as they were getting? Were they resentful or supportive?
It wasn’t good news.
(Side conversation)
How about hotels? Did the hotel gigs either open up or were they consistent through your career?
I had some, like the Meridien Hotel in Paris. I worked the Copley Plaza in Boston. Then I worked the Sheridan in New York. That was not too long.
Couple other holes I’d like to fill, the names of your second and third husbands?
Let’s see the second one was…what was that so-and-so’s name? Bill Miles.
And you married him approximately when?
And your third husband?
Walter Eady.
You married him…
And you’ve been divorced since when?
Since ’61.
Dorothy, they say that women always marry the same man over and over, were they all three alike?
Each one was different. They grew progressively worse. I should have kept the first one and not married the second and third.
When was the first one’s birthday?
January the 9th.
When was the second one’s birthday?
He was a Gemini, oh crazy. June 16th.
When was the third one?
He was November.
Now see, you have winter, summer and fall. Now maybe the fourth one should be from spring.

I don’t know. Three times, they trying to tell you something, ain’t they? Just don’t marry nobody. Stay single . . . I talked to Tommy Tucker and I said, “You getting married?” and he said, “I wouldn’t shack with Jackie Onassis.” He said, “I’m sick of doing time and marriage ain’t nothing but time. They come in pretty, acting nice and after they get you, they change.”
Can you tell me specifically what sacrifices you had to make as a musical artist because of those marriages?
I don’t remember making any sacrifices too much. But I think I should have just stayed single and just practiced the piano.
How about between marriages and having two sons, did you ever retire from the business?
No, it retired me for a while. This is a funny business. One day you’re Jay bird and the next day, the same day, you’re Jay Gould.
Have you found that to be true in that order, going from lacking popularity to becoming popular again? What would lead to those new peaks in popularity for you?
Well, in Chicago I had unpopularity, but I played for Delores Hope and we got a standing ovation, so I got popular again there. You can do a benefit sometimes and it awakens the promoters.
How about 1974, the tribute to Josephine Baker at Carnegie Hall. Did that represent kind of a new beginning in the ‘70’s for you?
Yes it did. Because I hadn’t played Carnegie Hall. I wanted to play on that with Thelma Carpenter, she really didn’t want me on the bill, but I was hired.
And what did the tribute to Josephine Baker consist of?
Me, Teddy Wilson and Thelma Carpenter.

(I want to) ask you about another experience at Carnegie Hall with Oscar Peterson. I understand there was a little bit of competition or rivalry, at least on his side, and not necessarily wanting to play after you. Can you tell me about that experience?

Did I play first? Or did he play first? The critic, John Wilson, said that my runs had come more to the point that his, that I enjoyed no popularity, they thought I should be reckoned in the same light that he is. They said that I had played just as well, maybe better.
Do you think of Oscar Peterson as your closest competition?
Sometimes I say that I’m more versatile than he is (laughs). He’s more predictable but he’s a great pianist. And he’s lost his left hand.
It’s the stroke. What do you most admire about Oscar Peterson?
He’s got a nice touch. He’s a big man of the piano, a giant.
He’s also an Art Tatum protégée.
No, he’s a Nat Cole protégée.
Interesting. Tell me about that. Take that a little bit further.
He heard Earl Hines first. So, he patterned his style after Earl Hines and Nat Cole. And he sings too.
How about touring around the world. I understand you’ve been not only to Europe, but to Africa, Asia and Australia.
I didn’t go to Australia and Africa. But I went to Japan.
Good to know. Tell me about the Japanese audience and how that differs from your experiences in the States and Europe.
They’re just like anybody else. If they move, they hit their derriere. I found that I could move them, too. I was happy about that.
When did you first go to Japan?
About three years ago. I’d gone before as a tourist.
How long did you perform there and where?
Six or seven days, in hotels and little bars no bigger than this. They charge $100 to come in and get a drink.
Who was booking this for you?
His name was Yoshi.
At what point did you begin playing with symphony orchestras?
And which orchestras have you played with?
New Orleans Symphony, and the Southeast Symphony and the Hollywood Symphony.
How did those come about?
When I got popular, they wanted me to play with the symphonies. That’s the way that comes about.
You said “when I got popular.” How did you become popular again?
That writer in the New York Times, New York Magazine, Whitney Balliett. Then I started getting all these good gigs, that don’t last too long and pay more money.
How does your performance fit into that program compared to your own either solo or trio performance.
I think playing with symphonies, you got to learn how to play with the other people, not run off. So I’m learning now how to play with people instead of playing for myself or with myself.

I wanted to ask you about some of the recordings you’ve made, starting in the ‘70’s perhaps. Several of these are recorded overseas, “Dorothy Donegan Trio,” “Live Best of Harlem,” recorded for the Four Leaf Clover label, recorded in Stockholm. Also, dates issued by Black and Blue in Paris, 1979. Another ’79 session in Paris for Black and Blue. Session for Ornament Records in Holland recorded in 1980, trio with Tony Mann on drums and Georg Lindzhes (?) on bass. You’ve got a session for Swingtime in Munich in 1980. A session in Zurich, Switzerland in 1986. Sounds like your European audience is really developing by the ‘70’s that all of these live sessions are being recorded there.
Yes. Well, people record in the trees. When they have a storm, they come out the trees. They snatch your music you know. A lot of things I recorded, I don’t remember recording.
Have you ever seen records released that you didn’t even know about?
Yes.
Talk to me about the royalty arrangements on those European sessions.
There’s nothing to talk about, you don’t get any royalties. Just memories. What did Babs Gonzales say? He said, “Kicks and no bread.”
Do those European recordings benefit you in any way?
I don’t know whether they do or not. I guess it makes one more person know you that didn’t.
Do you think that they helped you get bookings?
Not necessarily.
Very few sessions were recorded in the States of your music at this time. I saw one New York date. Why is it that the domestic recordings dried up?
I don’t know. Maybe they didn’t understand what I was doing.
Did you ever feel that you burned any bridges that you regret on the business side?
Mmm-hmmm.
Can you tell me about that.
Some of the booking agents I would burn the bridges, ‘cause I thought 10% of a dollar was a dime instead of sixty cents. But I understand, if they don’t steal, they won’t book you.

What wisdom can you pass on to other younger musicians, in particular women musicians, from your experience, the rough experiences you’ve had with recordings, with bookings and just making a living performing this music.

Well, I think they should go to school so they can get a job. ‘Cause if you can’t get a J.O.B. you’ll be a B.U.M. And if you don’t go to school you’ll be a fool. And then show business should be the second career.
How about…you talked about Tatum taking you on as mentor. Have you served as a mentor to other musicians?
I don’t think so. If I like somebody I’ll help them. But I don’t know. I think I’ll help people. I won’t show them everything but…
One of the words that occasionally comes up in writings about you especially in ‘70’s and ‘80’s is “feminist.” How do you feel about that word?
I think I still like for the name that pay the bills. I like that very much. I don’t want to pay the man’s bills. My money belongs to me and his belongs to him. I don’t want no pimps.
Some of the non-musical flourishes that you incorporate into your act, the hip shaking and all, does that go back to vaudeville influences, not necessarily with you…
It could be. We learned about Chippy Hill and Step ‘n’ Fetchit. Not Step ‘n’ Fetchit, Snake Hips Tucker.

That long tradition of vaudeville performance and entertainers, even going into Armstrong and Dizzy Gillespie, the clowning…tell me about those performance aspects with some of the vocal impersonations, could you tell me about that?
I could do Lena Horne and Ella, not Etta Jones, I keep calling her James sometimes. I can do Nellie Lutcher, Rose Murphy and a lot of them; Billie Holiday, especially.
I assumed the audience really loved that.
It breaks up the monotony of the music.
Tell me about breaking up the monotony of the music, the entertainment role that you also…
People have a retention span—you can’t play too much music. You have to learn how to cut off and cut on.

Why do you think it is that Oscar Peterson and George Shearing, Billy Taylor, Calvin Jackson, they can all sit down to play all night and not sing or shake hips and they always expect us to do something extra?
Well, if you can do something extra, then you should get two salaries.
I agree. But they don’t want to pay us as much but they want us to do extra.
Well, sometimes you sell a little records and make a little extra money, honey.
Maybe in the next world we’ll have a chance to sit down and just play like we want to play without extra.
They don’t ask me to do that.
I know that.
Sometimes if the music ain’t going too well, I’ll shake a little. But now I don’t do it too much.

Yes. But why do you think it is that Oscar Peterson and some of those other musicians, never had to, all they could do is sit there and play, Ahmad Jamal, anybody else you want to name and they don’t even have to smile.
Well, it depends on how the audience is liking it.
Why do you think it’s the fact that they don’t expect that from them?
I don’t know, there’s two sides to everything. Some women, like Shirley Horn, she sings. Have you heard her?
Yes.
Nellie Lutcher, (sings). Everybody’s got a gimmick.

In the early 1980’s, it seems another wave of popularity for you. “Women Blow Their Own Horns,” part of George Wein’s July 3, 1981 Kool Jazz Festival. Did that open new doors for you, expose you to a new audience?
Yes, and I think…that’s what they called the show? What’s his name, who wrote it?
George Wein produced it through Festival Productions.
Who was that writer?
Whitney Balliett?
That other writer.
I don’t know. But I’m sure you did steal the show.
Yeah, that’s what they said. Said I stole it two times.
Who were some of the other women on that performance, do you recall?
Marian McPartland, people like that you know.
It’s still pretty rare to see more than one woman jazz musician on stage at any time. Do you think that having an evening of performances by women artists, is that a good thing or not necessarily?
We don’t need it. Let them play with men, against men. There shouldn’t be a separate role for women and a separate role for men. They either can perform or they can’t.
Do you think that those all-women performances are more marketable to the people who are booking them?
They could be.

How about in the early 1990’s? It seems the cycle comes around every few years. New popularity. George Weins’ Kool Jazz Festival, at Carnegie Hall, Lorraine Gordon booking you into the Village Vanguard. Tell me about that.
What did I do at the Vanguard?
Is it a big deal that you’re playing at the Vanguard or is it just another gig?
It’s just another gig. They all are gigs.
These are a little more high profile. Do these high profile gigs help bring you new audiences?
Now I’m getting a Japanese audience.
Tell me about that.
They bring them there in droves. And they watch me and they seem to like it.
American Jazz Master Award from the National Endowment for the Arts, 1992. An honor for you? You’re smiling, tell me about that.
Somebody called me up, Antoinette Handy, called me up and she said, “I been looking for you for four weeks.” So I said, “Do I owe you money?” She said, “No, I have
something to give you.” I started crying. She said, “We got $20,000 for you.” I said, “Ohhhh, Ohhh.” She said, “It’s true.” So, that’s how I got that.
You mentioned honorary doctorates. What other awards and honors have you received? I remember Dorothy Donegan Day, your birthday, I think 1974 in Chicago, keys to the City, that type of thing.
Oh yeah, I get that in New Orleans and Chicago, too.
What awards have you received that you’re most proud of?
The doctorates. I like those better. When they gave me one, I said, “Ohhhhh.” I started crying. I said, “My husbands call me more than that.”
Hollywood Bowl performances with the symphony.

That went good. If I can’t get you one way, I can get you another. So, I got a standing ovation of 17,000 people. And Jeffery Hines, Gregory Hines, snatched the flowers out of my hand and ran off the stage.
Why did he do that?
I don’t know. I started to take my shoe and throw it.
[Did you] upstage Jeffery Hines and perhaps the symphony itself?
I think, yeah, them 17,000 people upstaged him. My ex-husband was there with two women and he was clapping.
It seems that you upstage just about anyone you perform on a bill with. How do you maintain a professional relationship with these people? Or do you just leave them behind?
Just leave them behind. They’ll call me again. Someone said, “I need her like Custer needed more Indians.”

I’d like to go through a list of piano players and just have you comment on them. What’s most significant about their playing in your mind? Why do they continue to be so influential? First, Jelly Roll Morton.
Great. He was a pioneer of boogie-woogie style of the blues. I didn’t know him.
How about Earl Hines?
I liked him. He played the rolling of the fingers, the trumpet style.
Art Tatum.
The master.
I guess there’s nothing else you can say about Tatum. Raymond Walters.
Oh, he was my idol. He showed me how to play like Art Tatum. He stayed drunk most of the time but he sure could play.
He was out of Chicago?
Yes.
What happened to him?
I don’t know. I been trying to find out every time I go to Chicago.
When he was showing you Tatum runs and fingering, was he right? Did he show you the same way Tatum showed you a few years later?
No, Tatum played five ways and you pick what you can gorilla.
Teddy Wilson.
He was the Mozart of the piano. He played very soft and fast.
Anything about his style that was incorporated into yours?
I liked him.
Cleo Brown.
She played a lot of rolls and bass. She had a good left hand.
Ellington.
Ellington could play with his band. I guess he could stride a little bit, couldn’t he? Him and Basie.
Basie was next.
I like Basie, especially the record of him and Oscar Peterson playing.
Erroll Garner.
Oh, he was the funkiest. I loved him. His music made you want to shake or dance.
Fats Waller.
I liked the way he played. He laid it down.
How about Fats Waller in that entertainer role?
I liked that too.
Did you learn anything from his approach to entertaining an audience?
I guess not, but I respected it.
How about in the same vein, Nellie Lutcher?
Well, she knew what she could do best. (sings—“He’s really gone…”)
Nellie Lutcher a good entertainer?
I think so. She’d have to be.
Meade Lux Lewis.
Good boogie-woogie.
Anything in particular about his style that stands out?
He could play it heavy.
Pete Johnson.
Same thing.
Albert Ammons.
Same thing.
Any difference between the three?
No, they all were great.
Who’s your favorite of the three?
All of them.
Nat Cole.
He could play like Earl Hines. And who else did he play like? Yeah, he played like Earl Hines.
Thelonious Monk.
He was an innovator.
How so?
He played different from everybody else. He was a creator.
Phineas Newborn.
He was a genius. He could play light and fast. He’d come over and challenge me all the time.
And how would those competitions go, those challenges?
I would hang in there with him. I put one of those concertos on him.
And? Did he make it, did he live up to your high standards?
Well, I liked him anyway. ‘Cause he could play in the bass with two hands, that running bass (sings). I liked him.
How about Bud Powell?
He was great, too.
In what way? How did his greatness differ from some of these other players?
I don’t know. But me and Erroll Garner heard him during his last days and he wasn’t doing too well, but I admired him when he was right. When he and Buttercup were together, you know.
How about Ahmad Jamal?
Oh, I love him.
What do you love about him?
I like the way he plays. I like Fritz. That’s his real name, you know.
How about Cecil Taylor?

He’s a screwball but he got a lot of technique. They wanted to put me and him together you know, they had done it with Mary Lou. So I told ‘em, I said, “I’ll steal that show if I have to pull up my dress.”
You mentioned a few of these people being geniuses. What does it take in Dorothy Donegan’s mind to be a genius?
Well, Cecil Taylor would be a genius in his way. And Ahmad Jamal. I guess geniuses, they know when they’re geniuses.
How about Dorothy Donegan—genius?
Uh-huh, I think so.
In what way?
In all ways.
What has Dorothy Donegan brought to the musical world that was not there before and will not be there after her?
There will just be more Dorothy Donegans coming up.
You think so? Where do you see that support coming from and how do you see the younger players coming through?
They’re beginning to listen now and they got to learn how to play with the left hand. See, before they didn’t know how to play with the left hand.
Tell me about your left hand, how it developed and how it changed over time.
Well, I was playing in the ‘30’s, so I met Buck and Bubbles. So, they said, “What you gonna do with the left hand?” I said, “I don’t know.” Said, “Did you leave it in the dressing
room? Say, woman, you’ve got to play some left hand.” So I think my left hand got stronger than my right.
How do you describe your own piano style?
Mine?
Yes.
I don’t know. A highly-trained jazz classical pianist.
You said jazz first. Would you prefer them to be equal? How would you, if you had to do it all over again, how would you like to be as a piano player? What directions did you not take…
I think I would play all classical. ‘Cause then I wouldn’t have to think about the jazz and making a living. In classical, you have to fill the halls. It’s not just wanting to be a classical pianist.
Dorothy, I’d like to ask you about some of your classical influences. What do you think of Chopin?
I love him. He must be played delicately, softly and fast. He’s a very difficult composer.
He sure is. What about Mendelssohn?
I like the “Rondo Cappricioso” and the “Caprice Brilliant” by Mendelssohn.
How about Beethoven?
I like him. He was very clever.
In what ways?
His harmonics.
His harmonics, yes. His left hand sounds like yours by the way. How about Grieg?
I like the Grieg Concerto and some of his other pieces. The Peer Gynt Suite.
How about Bach?
I like him, too. He stresses the independence of each finger.
You mean the two-part and three-part inventions?
Yeah, and then the other—what is is, the Well-Tempered Clavicord (sic).
How about Mozart?
I like him, he’s light.
What do you mean, light? Not difficult to play?
He’s difficult to play but he’s light, very light.
Can you tell me something—when you’re really, really down, which one of these do you prefer to play?
I like to work on the Rachmaninoff Third Concerto.
When you’re really down? What does it do for you?
I don’t know, there’s so many notes to play.
You know they say that you receive music sometimes through the crown of your head, sometimes through your throat, sometimes through your solar plexus. Is that what Rachmaninoff does for you?
He does everything. I think some of his music has some Negro spirituals in it.
You do?
Yes.
Which ones in particular?
Especially the Rachmaninoff Third. In some of his music you can hear themes that could be presented as jazz.
Like a universal language, huh?
(sings) That’s in the Rachmaninoff’s Second.
That’s true, “Full moon and empty arms.” Tell me something, have you always led a very clean life, I mean like food-wise… ?
Yes, no dope, no cigarettes, no drinking.
You never drank?
No, just Cherry Herring.
That’s a liqueur, very sweet.
That helped get the diabetes.
(laughs) Would you drink it straight or all through the night, or just have one drink at night or?
One or two or three. I like to pour it over ice cream.
Oh yeah, I hear you. So, you never drank or never smoked or never took dope.
No. One time I hit my own lamp post. Three times, and I said, “I’m hitting my own lamp post and I’m not a junkie.”
Well tell me, what vice do you have, my dear?
Just buy clothes. My ex-husband said, “I wish you wouldn’t be buying all these clothes.” I said, “Well I could have been a junkie.” He said, “Well, I wish you had, you’d a gone to sleep.”
So, shopping is your…
Outlet.
You get high when you get in the store, huh?
And I don’t have to look at the price tags, like the schoolteachers do. They look at the price tags and then they say they want it. But I got good taste.
You do have good taste.
You, too.
Thank you. I’d like to ask you another question. What are your hopes and wishes now?
I hope I get a million dollars, then I’ll quit the business.
Is that true? You would really quit the business?
Yes, the business ain’t what it’s cracked up to be.
If you had the million dollars, what would you do instead of playing?
I would play occasionally. I’d take gigs that I wanted, not gigs somebody else wanted me to do.
I think that sounds good to me, too. Because you come to such a point, don’t you?
Yeah, it’s time to quit. Lena, it’s time to quit. Sit down before you fall down.
So, you’ve played, you think, almost every place you wanted to and if you had a million dollars would you think of building your own self a club and playing in it?
Maybe I’d buy a club that’s already put up.
And then play when you get ready.
When I get ready. I call the shots.
I like that. I think that’s a very, very good way….
Like Artie Shaw, he quit. He took that clarinet and they said, broke it across a mirror.
Is that true? Artie Shaw.
When most of us, we played when we sick. Like Lionel Hampton, 80 years old, should be not working.
I think that’s keeping him alive, don’t you?
No, that’s keeping him tired. And somebody said, his manager stole his money.
Maybe that’s why he has to work.
Could be.
What other wish would you like, since this is your birthday?
To get well and sit down. Just travel.
Where would you go?
All over the world.
Would you like to live any other special place?
I could live in Switzerland a little while.
Have a chalet in Switzerland? Who would you like to listen to while you’re travelling? Is there any musician that you would especially like to drop in on?
I’d go hear Peterson, Martha Argerich, some of those Russian pianists play. I like to be real sharp, though. And then I like to go to Vegas.
Who would you like to listen to in Vegas?
I’d like to see the shows.

Well, I tell you, we’d like to thank you very much for these two days that we’ve spent with you and your birthday. On behalf of the Smithsonian, I’m certainly really glad we got you on tape, ‘cause you are my idol.
You’ve always been mine, you and Jo Jones.
Thanks a million.
That’s it?
[END]
